2.3.4  Strain Analyses

       With the indexing response of EBSD systems, each EBSD data point  is
associated with one value of crystal orientation. For strain analysis purposes, the
EBSD user can then correlate  this value with a specific type of twins or grain
boundaries, or this value can be used to calculate different strain parameters including
Taylor and Schmid  factors. With a good understanding of the EBSD technique
(system  calibration and sources of uncertainties),  precise and quantitative  strain
analyses can be performed with the indexing response of EBSD systems, which is not
the case of strain analyses achieved with the current intensity response of EBSD
systems. Indeed, strain analyses (or any microstructural analysis) with the intensity
response  are  generally performed by observing grey-tone  variations  in  intensity


                                                                      23tmages and by making correlations with the expected microstructure or the one
observed with indexing results or other characterization techniques. However, because
the EBSP quality and the intensity response are influenced by several experimental
conditions (see section 2.3.3), it is actually not possible to relate a specific grey-tone
to one type of strain mechanisms (crystal defects) or to a specific level of strain in a
material. Moreover,  as mentioned  section  2.2, exact properties of the  intensity
response of unknown  (e.g.  strain sensitivity, reproducibility, effects of the EBSP
processing steps). Consequently, only qualitative or semi-quantitative strain analyses
can actually be performed with the intensity response of EBSD systems.
       Very few authors have  tried to understand and to develop the  intensity
response of commercial EBSD systems  for  strain analyses of materials.  In  this
connection, Tucker et al. (2000) mentioned in a paper that commercial EBSD systems
"have tended to adopt only simple measures of pattern quality (intensity response),
presumably  in  order  to maximize  the  speed of orientation mapping  (indexing
response) which is seen as the primary use of the EBSD technique" [38]. On the other
hand, this situation may also be explained by the fact that EBSD technologies were
not appropriate in the 90s for achieving strain analyses based on the EBSP quality.
Indeed, until then, the resolution and sensitivity of EBSD cameras were not enough
advanced for acquiring good EBSP quality and/or for capturing slight changes in the
EBSP quality caused by the presence of strain in materials. Additionally, a lower
computer memory space may also explain the development of one EBSP processing
procedure rather than two (e.g. one for the indexing response and one for the intensity
response).
       Mackenzie et Dingley (1987) and Quested et al. (1988) were the first authors
to propose the use and quantification of the EBSP quality (then called pattern
diffuseness) as a mean for assessing dislocation contents in materials [39,40]. Indeed,
these authors showed that the visual aspect of EBSPs deteriorates when the strain
level of materials increased. Moreover, Mackenzie et Dingley found that the EBSP
quality could be well analysed by looking to frequency intensity variations in EBSPs
previously transformed into the Fourier space. Indeed, they showed that EBSPs of
high quality (un strained materials) show more high frequency intensity variations than
EBSPs of lower quality (deformed materials). Some years later, this F ourier approach
was reconsidered by Wilkinson et Dingley, who quantified the EBSP quality (pattern
diffuseness) by calculating the spectral first peak area (SFP A) and the power spectra

                                                                   24first moment (PSFM) of specific EBSP zone axes (e.g. <112»  [3]. These authors
found that these parameters (SFP A and PSFM) varied approximately linearly with the
amount of strain in a material (for a 6061 aluminum alloy).
        However, one major disadvantage of the previously-described techniques is
that they had to be performed manually and were thus time-consuming. Indeed, each
EBSP had to be recorded on a photographic film and then digitised before achieving
any strain analysis. Consequently, these techniques were not suitable for automatic
EBSD mapping. Today, with the emergence of new EBSD cameras and greater
computer memory space, Fourier image analysis techniques (and other image analysis
techniques) could be revisited and (quantitatively) compared to the current intensity
response of commercial EBSD  systems. Moreover,  these comparisons could be
extended to other definitions of the intensity response such as those studied by Tao
(2003) and Wright (2006) and which are based on Hough images of EBSPs (e.g.:
intensity mean, deviation and entropy of Hough images) [9,41].

        This  section  will provide information and explanations about  statistical
Design-Dj-Experiments (DOE) and analysis techniques. The reader  is referred to
Appendix A for the statistical terminology employed in this section and the next ones.


2.4.1  Factorial and Fractional Designs

Because the way data are collected (e.g.: factor levels; order and number of runs) has
a great influence on the validity and accuracy of results, designs are particularly
important for drawing meaningful conclusions about collected data [13]. Moreover,
efficiency in data collection is always an indirect goal of any industrial and scientific

## 3. grieken2005novelquantitativeproceduresa pages 139-158 (Context ID: pqac-00000023)

ies

A method was developed to calculate the characteristic X ray intensities from a paint bilayer
structure containing two layers of a mixture of commonly used white paints (ZnO, PbO,
BaSO4, TiO2). For Ti and Zn the Kα and Kβ lines, for Pb the Lα and Lβ lines, and for Ba the
Ll, Lα, Lβ1, Lβ2, Lγ1 and Lγ2,3 lines are incorporated. The model can easily be extended to
further materials and X ray lines. The method was applied for a system composed of ZnO and
PbO. X ray spectra taken from several paintings have shown the simultaneous presence of
these paints. The important question is immediately raised whether the paints were mixed
together or painted one over another. Taking into account that the energy dependent X ray
attenuation is different in the two cases, the measurement of the relative line intensities could
provide information in this respect. In the particular situation where an infinitely thick PbO
layer is covered by a ZnO layer of increasing thickness, our calculation shows that in the case
of mixing no change can be expected in the Pb–Lβ/Pb–Lα ratio. If the ZnO layer is painted
onto the PbO layer, on the other hand, this ratio is rapidly increasing, as displayed in Fig. 20.
The very interesting fact that this relative line intensity is constant in the case of mixture is
due to a lucky accident: the ratios of the mass attenuation coefficients for the Pb–Lα and Pb–
Lβ in PbO and ZnO are practically the same.

3.5. Dosimetric tests

The non-destructiveness of the method is based on the fact that the energy transferred is too
negligible to cause any damage. But even the mention of any chance of a radiation hazard, on
the other hand, is a rather inhibiting factor for allowing the spectrometer to enter a public
collection. In order to gain reassuring information, the radiation dose around the source-
detector assembly was checked in two ways. Using a hand-held dosimeter, measurements
were made around the analysed spot at different distances. Figure 21 shows the result of a
measurement in the vicinity of the 109Cd excitation head. The dosimeter indicates 8 µSv/h.
Taking into account the radiation shielding of the radioactive sources, no significant dose was
expected, and these rough tests have confirmed the expectations. In addition, long term dose
measurements were also carried out using a fixed arrangement of TTL tablets. Ten tablets
were put onto a wooden stick grid around the excitation head (Fig. 22.) and exposed to the
radiation for 5 days for both the 109Cd and 241Am sources. The highest value obtained was
about 13 µSv/h. The dose rate level at distances longer than 20 cm was below the detection
limit.

3.6. Miscellaneous

Our  laboratory  took  part  in  the  Proficiency  Test  Exercise  for XRF  Laboratories
(PTXRFIAEA/01) organized by the IAEA. We also participated in the GeoPT International
proficiency test organized by Dr. Phil Potts. The evaluation of the test run is ongoing.


1324. Summary

The work within the frame and with financial support of the CRP has essentially followed the
intentions of the detailed plan. A rather versatile portable XRF spectrometer with radioisotope
excitation was built. The heart of the spectrometer is an AMPTEK XR-100CR X ray detector
together with the matching PXT/CR power supply and amplifier. Compact excitation heads
containing 55Fe, 109Cd and 241Am radiation can be alternatively used to cover the widest
elemental range. The system was applied for real in situ analysis of paint layers. Taking into
account that the samples to be analysed were unique precious samples, sample preparation
and calibration processes for general use could not be specified in this particular application
of the in situ use of XRF. Instead of more or less useless efforts to make general calibrations,
our work was focused on contributing to the solution of the important practical problem when
Ti (Ti white) has to be detected or its presence excluded. A calculation method was also
developed in order to gain information from the relative X ray line intensity. Mainly due to
administrative difficulties, the planned pilot studies in a public collection had to be postponed
and it was not possible to carry out the planned measurements on painted stone archaeological
objects. Instead of these measurements, interesting applications were found with the help of

Abstract

Portable energy-dispersive X ray fluorescence equipment, mainly composed of a small sized X ray tube and
thermoelectrically cooled X ray detector, were employed to analyse paintings. The frescos of Giotto in the
chapel of the Scrovegni in Padua were analysed, and oil paintings by De Chirico, of which 15 of certain
attribution, and 11 supposedly painted by De Chirico. The pollution effects on the Giotto frescos were
determined by analysing sulphur on the surface, and the thickness and composition of golden haloes were also
measured. The 11 oil paintings by De Chirico are possibly fakes, on the basis of the different fingerprints of
authentified and unauthentified paintings.

1. Introduction

Energy dispersive X ray fluorescence (EDXRF) analysis is a non destructive, multielemental
and simple technique which is based on irradiation of a sample by a low intensity X ray beam,
and on detection of secondary X rays emitted by the sample. The energy of these secondary
X rays is characteristic of the elements present in the sample, and the intensity is proportional
to their concentration. The thickness of the sample involved in the analysis depends on the
element, on the matrix and on the energy of the primary and secondary radiation.

The typical portable equipment for EDXRF analysis is composed basically of an X ray tube,
an X ray detector with related electronics and a multichannel analyser.

EDXRF systems are very useful for analysis of works of art, because the analysis is non-
destructive, multielemental, simple and relatively inexpensive. Portability of the systems is
almost mandatory. In fact, in very few cases it is possible to study a work of art outside its
normal location (museum, church, excavation, etc.).

There are many materials as well as a variety of problems in archaeometry that can be studied
by using an EDXRF apparatus. There are then cases in which a qualitative or a semi-
quantitative analysis is sufficient (for example in the case of paintings); in this case it is more
important to know the relative amount of an element in different points of the surface and/or
at different depths, than to quantitatively determine the chemical elements.

Recently developed thermoelectrically cooled semiconductor detectors, such as Si-PIN, Si-
drift, CdZnTe, CdTe and HgI2, coupled to miniaturized low-power, dedicated X ray tubes, are
well suited for assembling portable systems for EDXRF analysis of archaeological samples.

In this paper, EDXRF analysis of Giotto’s frescos in the Chapel of the Scrovegni in Padua is
described, as well as that of 26 oil paintings by De Chirico or ascribed to De Chirico.

A typical portable EDXRF system is mainly composed of:

•  an X ray tube,
•  an X ray detector with electronics,
•  a multi-channel analyser.

2.1. X ray tubes

A great variety of X ray tubes of various types (anode, maximum voltage, current), size and
cost are currently available for EDXRF analysis, depending on the problem, and more
specifically on the element or elements, to be analysed. Low-power X ray tubes with selected
anodes are generally adequate. They may be chosen primarily as a function of the atomic
number of the elements to be analysed. Table I gives a survey of useful portable X ray tubes
[1–2].

A small sized, low power W-anode X ray tube working up to 40 kV, 0.1 mA, is adequate for
analysis of almost all elements of archaeometric interest. Working at low voltages (5–10 kV)
or at high voltages (35–40 kV), this tube is able to excite low atomic number elements such as
S and Cl, or elements from Ca to Pb, respectively [2] (Fig. 1).

2.2. X ray detectors [3]

In the last few years, small sized thermoelectrically cooled semiconductor detectors have
become available, such as Si-PIN [3], Si-drift [4], CZT [3-5], CdTe [3–6] and HgI2 [7–8].

These detectors are cooled to about –30°C by means of a Peltier circuit, and are contained in
small sized boxes also including a high quality preamplifier and the Peltier circuit.

HgI2 detectors were the first to be constructed and have currently an energy resolution of
about 180–200 eV at 5.9 keV, and an efficiency of about 100% in the whole range of X rays.

Si-PIN detectors, with an Si thickness of 300–500 µm, exhibit an energy resolution of 160–
200 eV, and are useful up to about 25 keV because of the decreasing efficiency versus energy,
due to the limited thickness. Because of the high shaping time of the amplifier (12 µm) these
detectors are also not convenient for high counting rates.




154Si-drift detectors have an Si thickness of 300 µm and an energy resolution of about 140–
150 eV at 5.9 keV. They are able to work also at high counting rates.

CZT detectors have a typical thickness of 2 mm and an efficiency of about 100% in the whole
X ray range. The energy resolution is about 300 and 700 eV at 5.9 and 59.6 keV, respectively.

3. Theoretical background

A painting may be considered as a succession of pigment layers. In a fresco, over the plaster
there is a preparation layer, and then one or more pigment layers. In an oil painting, over the
canvas there  is a preparation layer, and then, again, one or more pigment layers. The
penetration of incident and output radiation is determined by exponential laws of the type e

incident and output radiation, multiplied by the thickness of the layer. The thickness of a
pigment layer is generally very low, and therefore the exponential may be reduced to (1 – µx).

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a compact proposal-ready evidence table with columns: technique/acquisition choice, quantitative fidelity effect, interpretation for metal-alloy microanalysis, and source context IDs. Include SEM-EDS standards \u00b15% vs standardless up to \u00b130%; overvoltage >=1.8 and 35\u00b0 detector geometry; dead time 10\u201320%; standardless and standards-based NIST alloy errors; EBSD scan-speed indexing rates 54 vs 154 PPS, frame averaging 1/5/10/20/30 and sixfold speed gain, 10/20/30 kV, resolutions, phase-list zero-correct case; micro-XRF 15\u201350 kV, 12\u2013106 \u00b5A and filter thicknesses, 10\u2013100 ppm MDLs, and Mg Al-alloy errors of 40% and 5000%. Clearly label where evidence is transferable rather than LPBF AlSi10Mg-specific."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Technique/acquisition choice | Quantitative fidelity effect | Interpretation for metal-alloy microanalysis | Source context IDs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SEM-EDS: standards-based vs standardless** | Physical standards can support about **±5% relative uncertainty**; standardless analysis can reach **±30%**, and normalization to 100% can conceal errors. | Standards are needed for qualification-grade alloy chemistry; standardless results should be treated as semi-quantitative. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020) |
| **SEM-EDS: accelerating voltage/overvoltage** | ISO 22309 specifies incident energy of at least **1.8× the selected X-ray-line energy**; adequate Fe-K excitation, for example, requires at least **12 kV**. Measurements at **5, 10, and 20 kV** produced substantial composition scatter in a low-energy-line test material. | Voltage determines excitation efficiency and interaction volume; one fixed voltage is not valid for every alloying element. | (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) |
| **SEM-EDS: take-off geometry** | Quantitative protocols require a flat surface normal to the beam and approximately **35° to the EDS detector**. Low take-off angles at holes and grooves reduced integral counts and the number of detected elements. | Tilt, roughness, pores, and melt-pool relief can create element-dependent absorption errors, especially for low-energy Mg and Al lines. | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000019) |
| **SEM-EDS: beam current/dead time** | Beam current and dead time were identified as dominant variables; **10–20% dead time** was recommended. In standards-based work, beam-current drift was held to **0.2%** over a **20 min** session. | Too little current gives poor counting statistics, while excessive rate causes pile-up and dead-time losses; current must be measured or controlled. | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000020) |
| **SEM-EDS: normalized standardless NIST Fe-Cr-Ni alloy** | At **20 kV**, errors were **+1.3% Cr, −0.4% Fe, and −0.8% Ni**; on another system at **25 kV**, they were **−3.1%, +1.3%, and −4.1%**. | Even favorable major-element results vary with detector calibration, fitting, matrix corrections, and factory databases. | (pqac-00000019) |
| **SEM-EDS: unnormalized standardless vs standards** | Unnormalized standardless analysis gave **−0.7% Cr, −2.3% Fe, and −2.7% Ni** and totaled **98.1 wt%**. Physical standards reduced errors to **<1%** against NIST EDS values, although residual uncertainty versus wet chemistry was **3–7%** because of ZAF corrections. | Standards cancel much of the beam-current, geometry, detector-efficiency, and contamination dependence, but matrix-correction uncertainty remains. | (pqac-00000020) |
| **SEM-EDS: Mg in LPBF AlSi10Mg** | **Evidence gap:** no controlled SEM-EDS parameter sweep for minor Mg in LPBF AlSi10Mg was found. General evidence places standardless uncertainty as high as **±30%**, with greater risk for low-energy/light-element peaks. | Apparent Mg differences in AlSi10Mg cannot reliably be assigned to metallurgy without alloy- and instrument-specific validation. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020) |
| **EBSD: scan speed—transferable metal evidence** | Increasing speed from **54 to 154 patterns/s** reduced conventional indexing success from **34.9% to 9.3%**. At 54 patterns/s, processing raised success to **41.3–59.7%**; at 154 patterns/s, improved values reached approximately **12.5–37.6%**. | Faster mapping can turn most pixels into non-indexed or unreliable measurements and make grain statistics cleanup-dependent. | (pqac-00000009) |
| **EBSD: frame averaging/exposure—transferable metal evidence** | Tests used **1, 5, 10, 20, and 30 frames**. One-frame patterns were almost entirely misclassified; improvement began at five, reasonable classification appeared at ten, and nearly all patterns were correct at 20–30. Five instead of 30 frames yielded a **6× speed gain** with high accuracy for most phases. | Exposure must be optimized against throughput rather than minimized; map appearance alone does not establish fidelity. | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| **EBSD: accelerating voltage—transferable metal evidence** | At **10, 20, and 30 kV**, 10 kV caused many misclassifications, 20 kV was the default, and 30 kV gave reasonably good performance. | Lower voltage can improve spatial resolution but reduce indexing reliability unless current, exposure, and indexing are re-optimized. | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| **EBSD: resolution/binning—transferable Al evidence** | Al 7075 was mapped at **5, 10, and 20 kV** using **4×4 and 8×8 binning**. Another study tested **156×128, 622×512, and 1244×1024** patterns; low resolution retained high accuracy for most phases but affected similar structures more strongly. | Binning accelerates acquisition but removes diffraction detail; suitability is phase- and microstructure-dependent. | (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| **EBSD: phase-list selection—transferable duplex-alloy evidence** | With two correct phases, Hough indexing produced a high-fidelity map. Expanding the list to **12 candidates** caused **zero patterns** to index as either correct phase despite ideal acquisition settings. | Phase-list choice can overwhelm improvements in beam conditions and generate confident but false phase maps. | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) |
| **EBSD: LPBF Al-Si-specific evidence** | **Evidence gap:** retrieved LPBF AlSi10Mg studies did not provide controlled factorial data for indexing rate or confidence versus current, voltage, exposure, binning, and phase list. | Published settings are examples, not validated optima; systematic LPBF Al-Si acquisition-response data are needed. | (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016) |
| **Micro-XRF: voltage/current/filters** | A commercial alloy protocol used **15–50 kV**, **12–106 µA**, and automatic filters of **75 µm Cu/25 µm Ti/200 µm Al**, **38 µm Al**, **25 µm Ti/300 µm Al**, or **25 µm Fe**. A **60 s** measurement comprised separate **30 s** light- and heavy-element scans. | Excitation must be element- and matrix-specific; a high-voltage transition-metal setting is not automatically sensitive to Mg, Al, or Si. | (pqac-00000028) |
| **Micro-XRF: current, optics, and filter sensitivity** | Tests used **40 kV/0.2 mA**, increased current from **0.2 to 1.0 mA** on Ag-Cu alloy, and evaluated **12.5–50 µm Mo** and **50–200 µm Al** filters. Polycapillary spectra were **35–40×** more intense than monocapillary spectra, with flux-density gain up to approximately **300×**. | Current controls photon statistics until rate limits intervene; filters and optics reshape both background and elemental sensitivity. | (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022) |
| **Micro-XRF: detection limits** | At **40 kV/0.2 mA** and **1000 s**, minimum detection limits were typically **10–100 ppm**; examples included **23–68 ppm Mn**, **10–22 ppm Rb**, and **68–94 ppm Ca**, depending on tube and optics. | Trace sensitivity cannot be transferred between instruments without documenting tube, optics, filter, atmosphere, detector, and live time. | (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022) |
| **Micro-XRF: matrix correction/calibration** | With suitable matrix-matched calibration, typical errors can fall below **5% for major** and **6% for some minor elements**. Without suitable standards, errors were typically below **50% for major/minor** and up to **100% for trace elements**, with some exceeding 100%. | Fundamental-parameter corrections do not remove matrix dependence; alloy-specific reference materials remain necessary. | (pqac-00000007) |
| **XRF: Mg errors in Al alloys—transferable to AlSi10Mg risk** | In AlMg4.5Mn0.7, EDXRF over-reported Mg by about **2 wt%**, approximately **40% relative**. In nominal Al99.5, it reported **0.196 wt% instead of 0.004 wt%**, a **5000% relative deviation**. | Minor/trace Mg can be grossly biased in commercial alloy modes. These cases are XRF—not SEM-EDS—and are not LPBF-specific, but quantify the light-element risk in Al matrices. | (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029) |
| **Expertise dependence and sparse rationale** | Operators remain responsible for checking artefact peaks and background fits. EBSD quality definitions are vendor-specific and partly documented; parameter effects remain incompletely quantified. Manufacturer-constrained software prevented investigators from identifying why two systems produced different standardless accuracies. | Standards and vendor defaults provide thresholds and operating envelopes, but not transparent alloy-specific response models; optimization remains instrument-, specimen-, and operator-dependent. | (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) |


*Table: Proposal-ready quantitative evidence linking SEM-EDS, EBSD, and micro-XRF acquisition choices to measurement fidelity in metal alloys. Transferable evidence and the absence of controlled LPBF AlSi10Mg parameter studies are explicitly identified.*

Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer: [artifact-00]

Context IDs that may be cited: [pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029]

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

Use the tools to answer the question: Provide quantitative, citable evidence on how acquisition parameter choices determine data fidelity in SEM-based microanalysis of metal alloys, suitable for the needs statement of a funding proposal. Cover: (1) standardless SEM-EDS quantification error and its dependence on accelerating voltage, beam current/dead time, take-off geometry, and standards-based vs standardless mode, including documented cases of large errors for minor/trace elements (e.g., Mg in AlSi10Mg or similar Al alloys); (2) EBSD indexing success rate and confidence index dependence on beam current, accelerating voltage, pattern exposure/binning, and phase-list selection, especially for additively manufactured (laser powder bed fusion) Al-Si alloys; (3) micro-XRF quantification sensitivity to tube voltage, current, filters, and matrix corrections for metal alloys; (4) published evidence that acquisition parameter selection remains trial-and-error and expertise-dependent, and that the rationale behind recommended settings in standards (e.g., ASTM E1508, ISO 22309) and vendor guides is sparsely documented or hard to access. Give specific numbers with citations.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
Abstract Recent developments in X-ray optics have allowed the development of a range of commercially available benchtop micro-XRF (μ-XRF) instruments that can produce X-ray spot sizes of 20-30 μm on the sample, allowing major- and trace-element analysis on a range of sample types and sizes with minimal sample preparation. Such instruments offer quantitative analysis using fundamental parameter based ‘standardless’ quantification algorithms. The accuracy and precision of this quantitative analysis on geological materials, and application of micro-XRF to wider geological problems is assessed using a single benchtop micro-XRF instrument. Quantitative analysis of internal reference materials and international standards shows that such instruments can provide highly reproducible data but that, for many silicate materials, standardless quantification is not accurate.Accuracy can be improved, however, by using a simple type-calibration against a reference material of similar matrix and composition. Qualitative analysis with micro-XRF can simplify and streamline sample characterization and processing for subsequent geochemical and isotopic analysis.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Systematic discrepancies persist between results from grain size measurement standards, such as ASTM E 112 and ASTM E 2627, when different imaging techniques and analysis methods are used. The source of these discrepancies may be differences in imaging physics, resolution limits, grain boundary definitions, post-processing practices, or combinations thereof. Geometric distortions and drift effects in scanning electron microscope imaging are systematically modeled using synthetic microstructures to assess their impact on electron backscatter diffraction-based grain size measurement accuracy. Standard methods are compared to a lesser-known method, the Triple Point Count (TPC). Most distortion types introduce smaller biases than the expected accuracy of the methods under typical imaging conditions. TPC provides consistent performance across varying resolutions and sampling conditions. This provides further evidence that reported discrepancies are largely driven by an assumption made in the estimate for converting intercept measurements to ASTM grain size numbers, as recently reported by Evans et al.</jats:p>

Influence of silicon morphology on direct current plasma electrolytic oxidation process in AlSi10Mg alloy produced with laser powder bed fusion Valid Text Names: 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 1-2', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 2-3', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 3-4', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 4-5', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 5-8', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 8-10', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 10-13', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 13-15', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 15-16', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 16-17', 'pezzato2022influenceofsilicon pages 17-17' BibTex: @article{pezzato2022influenceofsilicon, author = "Pezzato, L. and Gennari, C. and Franceschi, M. and Brunelli, K.", title = "Influence of silicon morphology on direct current plasma electrolytic oxidation process in AlSi10Mg alloy produced with laser powder bed fusion", year = "2022", journal = "Scientific Reports", volume = "12", month = "Aug", doi = "10.1038/s41598-022-18176-x", url = "https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18176-x", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "1", issn = "2045-2322" } Abstract: In this work, plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO) process was applied on AlSi10Mg samples, produced with laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), in the as printed condition and after different heat treatments, and, for comparison, on as-cast samples of AlSi10Mg. PEO process was performed in direct-current mode using high current densities and short time in a basic silicate electrolyte. For the first time, the effects of silicon morphology in L-PBF AlSi10Mg samples, in as printed condition and after different heat treatments, on the obtained PEO coating were investigated in terms of microstructure and corrosion properties. The microstructure of the substrate was characterized with optical and electron microscopy observations (optical microscopy OM, scanning electron microscopy SEM, and transmission electron microscopy TEM) and with X-ray diffraction (XRD). The analysis showed that heat treatments of annealing and solution treating modified the morphology and distribution of silicon in the samples obtained through L-PBF. The PEO coated samples were characterized with SEM, both on the surface and in the cross-section, and compositional analysis were performed with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analysis and elemental mapping. The coatings were also analyzed with XRD and the corrosion properties evaluated through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests. Also microhardness tests were performed on the substrates and on the coatings. The microstructure of the coatings was strongly influenced by the silicon distribution. In particular, a non-uniform distribution of silicon and the presence of iron-rich intermetallic (obtained in the as-cast and solution treated samples) induced the formation of more porous and thinner coatings in comparison with the ones obtained in the as printed and annealed samples. The not-uniform silicon distribution produced a not-homogenous distribution of silicon into the coatings. The particular cellular structure of the as printed sample induced the formation of a coating with a higher amorphous fraction, in comparison with the ones produced on the other samples. The higher thickness and lower porosity of the coatings obtained on the annealed and as printed samples resulted in an increase of the corrosion resistance. Evolution of Microstructure, Texture and Corrosion Properties of Additively Manufactured AlSi10Mg Alloy Subjected to Equal Channel Angular Pressing (ECAP) Valid Text Names: 'snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 1-2', 'snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 2-4', 'snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 4-6', 'snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 6-9', 'snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 9-12', 'snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 12-14', 'snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 14-16', 'snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 16-18', 'snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 18-19' BibTex: @article{snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure, author = "Snopiński, Przemysław and Woźniak, Anna and Łukowiec, Dariusz and Matus, Krzysztof and Tański, Tomasz and Rusz, Stanislav and Hilšer, Ondřej", title = "Evolution of Microstructure, Texture and Corrosion Properties of Additively Manufactured AlSi10Mg Alloy Subjected to Equal Channel Angular Pressing (ECAP)", year = "2022", journal = "Symmetry", volume = "14", pages = "674", month = "Mar", doi = "10.3390/sym14040674", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/sym14040674", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "4", issn = "2073-8994" } Abstract: In the selective laser melting process (SLM), the region irradiated by the laser beam is melted and quickly solidified, forming solidification lines (laser scan tracks) with symmetrical shapes. Because of the unique (rapid) crystallization conditions, the subgrain structures, typically observed inside these solidification lines, could also have variable geometric symmetrical patterns, e.g., cellular, pentagonal, or hexagonal cellular. The existence of such distinctive microstructures in SLM-made alloys has a significant impact on their superior mechanical and corrosion properties. Thus, any modification of this symmetrical microstructure (due to post-processing) can degrade or improve the properties of SLM-fabricated alloys. This study presents the experimental results on the effects of heat treatment and ECAP on microstructure modification and corrosion behavior of SLM-fabricated AlSi10Mg alloy. Light microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) were used for microstructural analysis. The corrosion properties of the given samples were determined using open-circuit potential (OCP), potentiodynamic polarization, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) techniques. EBSD observations showed that the imposed strain resulted in an obvious reduction in grain size to ~1.42 µm and ~0.24 µm after the first and second ECAP passes, respectively. Electrochemical tests revealed that the corrosion resistance of the ECAP-processed AlSi10Mg alloy improved significantly, which was confirmed by a nobler Ecorr and lower Icorr values, and higher polarization resistance. The final results indicated that the strain-induced crystalline defects provided more nucleation sites for the formation of a denser and thicker oxide film, thus enhancing the corrosion resistance of the AlSi10Mg alloy. Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000000

From text 'teng2020highresolutionxray pages 102-106'.

C Teng. High resolution x-ray imaging and quantitative microanalysis in electron microscopy. Unknown journal, 2020.

This excerpt provides quantitative evidence for SEM-EDS f-ratio quantification in Mg-Al-Zn systems, including an Mg45-Al27-Zn28 cast alloy and a Mg-Al-Zn diffusion alloy. The method combines EDS measurements with Monte Carlo simulations and uses calibration factors derived from known standards. Earlier binary Cu-Au work is reported to achieve accuracy better than 5% using beam-energy-dependent calibration factors, and the f-ratio method is described as more accurate than routine standardless analysis. Standardless analysis avoids real standards and electron-dose measurements, but its quantification accuracy is greatly undermined. The f-ratio method is specifically reported to be insensitive to beam-current stability because paired X-ray intensities are acquired from the same spectrum; consequently, it is suitable for long acquisitions and unstable currents. Experiments used both a cold field-emission SEM and a tungsten-emission SEM to investigate beam-current effects. The excerpt does not provide numerical comparisons involving accelerating voltage, count rate, detector dead time, take-off angle, specimen tilt, minor/trace Mg errors in Al or AlSi10Mg, EBSD, micro-XRF, or ASTM/ISO/vendor optimization guidance. It notes that energy-dependent calibration factors improve accuracy and that pure-element standards require beam current and acquisition time to be measured so simulations reproduce the electron dose.


---

## pqac-00000001

From text 'teng2020highresolutionxray pages 106-111'.

C Teng. High resolution x-ray imaging and quantitative microanalysis in electron microscopy. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt provides methodological evidence relevant to SEM-EDS quantification, particularly comparisons among f-ratio, standardless, and standards-based approaches, but it does not report numerical accuracy errors or results for Mg, AlSi10Mg, accelerating voltage, count rate, dead time, take-off angle, or specimen tilt. The f-ratio method uses Monte Carlo simulations to relate composition to elemental f-ratios; simulated intensities are calibrated using either pure-element (PE) standards or a standard compound. The excerpt states that PE-standard calibration requires measuring beam current and acquisition time during standard acquisitions so that simulated X-ray emission uses the same electron dose. For experiments, a Faraday cup/picoammeter measured beam current before and after each 300 s point acquisition on PE standards. The study deliberately used a field-emission SEM with unstable beam current and a tungsten-emission SEM with relatively stable current to investigate beam-current stability effects. The Mg-Al-Zn alloy was analyzed at 20 kV over 253 × 189 µm² areas with a 300 s live time, using both SEMs and multiple quantification methods. Its reference composition was 44.74 wt.% Mg, 27.76 wt.% Al, and 27.50 wt.% Zn by ICP-AES. No evidence is provided here concerning EBSD, micro-XRF, ASTM/ISO guidance, operator dependence, or trial-and-error optimization.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'kallio2025accuracyandprecision pages 59-62'.

M Kallio. Accuracy and precision comparison with elemental analysis parameter optimization for xrf, oes, and sem-eds. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt provides limited but directly citable evidence on SEM-EDS acquisition and quantification limitations. It reports a detection limit of 0.10 wt% and therefore recommends that EDS analysis be treated as qualitative rather than quantitative relative to OES. Geometry is identified as an important source of error: alignment of holes and grooves significantly affected integral counts and the number of identified elements, because a low take-off angle prevents X-ray detection. Among operating variables, beam current and SEM intensity, together with EDS dead time, are described as having the greatest effect on elemental-analysis results. The recommended EDS dead-time range is 10–20%, corresponding in the reported setup to a beam-intensity setting of 15–17. The excerpt also documents false elemental identifications from spectral overlap between Mo La and S Ka peaks; improved spectral resolution using WDS is suggested as a remedy. It does not provide numerical accuracy/error comparisons versus accelerating voltage, specimen tilt, standards-based versus standardless quantification, or specific Mg-in-Al/AlSi10Mg results. It likewise contains no EBSD indexing data, micro-XRF parameter studies, or explicit discussion of ASTM E1508, ISO 22309, vendor guidance, trial-and-error optimization, or operator dependence.

## pqac-00000003

From text 'teng2020highresolutionxray pages 44-49'.

C Teng. High resolution x-ray imaging and quantitative microanalysis in electron microscopy. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt provides quantitative evidence about thin-film and bulk EDS/X-ray quantification, particularly the effects of specimen thickness, beam-current stability, electron-dose measurement, and standards. The basic Cliff–Lorimer approach requires absorption and fluorescence corrections when the specimen is not sufficiently thin; calculating these corrections requires specimen thickness, which is difficult to measure accurately and can introduce uncertainty. The ζ-factor method determines composition and thickness simultaneously and is theoretically independent of electron dose, composition, and thickness, but it requires accurate measurement of total electron dose and is therefore unsuitable for unstable beam current. The f-ratio method was specifically developed for unstable-current systems such as cold-field-emission instruments. It uses intensity ratios from the same spectrum to suppress beam-current effects and combines conventional EDS with Monte Carlo simulation. Compound standards containing all target elements make quantification beam-current independent, while pure-element and other standards have also been investigated. Certified minerals containing up to five elements were quantified with satisfactory accuracy, and the limited reported f-ratio applications achieved better than 5% accuracy using beam-energy-dependent calibration factors. The excerpt does not provide numerical comparisons for Mg in Al or AlSi10Mg, SEM-EDS count rate/dead time, take-off angle or tilt, EBSD, micro-XRF, or ASTM/ISO/vendor optimization guidance.

## pqac-00000004

From text 'teng2020highresolutionxray pages 132-136'.

C Teng. High resolution x-ray imaging and quantitative microanalysis in electron microscopy. Unknown journal, 2020.

This excerpt provides directly citable evidence about SEM-EDS quantitative analysis, particularly the f-ratio method, accelerating voltage, acquisition time, beam-current handling, and standard-based versus standardless approaches. The f-ratio method combines conventional EDS acquisition with Monte Carlo simulation and uses calibration factors derived from standards of known composition. Previous applications cited in the excerpt reportedly achieved accuracy better than 5% (expressed as “less than 5%”), but the calibration factors were beam-energy dependent. In the described mineral-specimen experiment, ten point spectra were acquired at 10, 15, and 20 kV with 300 s live time, and at 25 and 30 kV with 200 s live time. Beam current was measured before and after each acquisition using a Faraday cup, with the average used to estimate total electron dose; no numerical beam-current, count-rate, or detector dead-time values are provided. The study compared f-ratio, INCA standardless and standard-based analysis, and DTSA-II standard-based k-ratio analysis. Oxygen was calculated stoichiometrically for all standard-based analyses. The excerpt also states that calibration factors derived from element intensities within one spectrum are independent of beam current, while compound standards can make the overall process beam-current independent. It does not provide evidence concerning Mg-in-Al or AlSi10Mg, specimen tilt/take-off angle, EBSD, micro-XRF, or ASTM/ISO/vendor recommendations.

## pqac-00000005

From text 'tong2026measurementuncertaintiesof pages 12-15'.

V. Tong and K. Mingard. Measurement uncertainties of energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy in the scanning electron microscope (SEM-EDX/EDS). National Physical Laboratory, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.47120/npl.mat135, doi:10.47120/npl.mat135.

The excerpt provides directly citable evidence about SEM-EDX/EDS acquisition variables and quantification limitations, but not about EBSD indexing, micro-XRF, specimen tilt/take-off angle, beam current, dead time, Mg-in-Al or AlSi10Mg specifically, or standards-based versus standardless quantification. For ionic-liquid PMIM NTf2, System B spectra were collected at 5, 10, and 20 kV with live times from 2.4 to 43.2 s; peak intensities changed strongly with accelerating voltage, whereas live time had only a minor effect on count rates. In a separate System A comparison at 5 kV and 120 s live time, changing detector channel bin widths from 5 to 10 eV broadened peaks and reduced their height by approximately 20%, while 2.5–5 eV spectra were similar. The excerpt also documents calibration limitations: System B was miscalibrated below 1 keV but correct above 2 keV. For NIST S479a, certified values differed from NIST EDX results by -6.6% for Cr, +1.0% for Fe, and +3.7% for Ni; the report attributes systematic deviations mainly to inadequate ZAF fluorescence correction, especially for strongly fluorescing Cr. It explicitly limits the uncertainty assessment to uncertainties within the EDX method rather than agreement with certified composition.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'tong2026measurementuncertaintiesof pages 15-18'.

V. Tong and K. Mingard. Measurement uncertainties of energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy in the scanning electron microscope (SEM-EDX/EDS). National Physical Laboratory, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.47120/npl.mat135, doi:10.47120/npl.mat135.

This excerpt provides limited but directly relevant evidence for SEM-EDS acquisition and semi-quantitative limitations. For qualitative analysis, the report recommends an accelerating voltage giving electron energy at least 1.8 times the relevant X-ray peak energy; it also specifies a specimen surface normal to the electron beam and at 35° to the EDX detector. For normalised standardless analysis, the candidate elements must be known, hydrogen and unidentified elements must be absent, and all quantified elements are recommended to have atomic number greater than 11. The method is explicitly inappropriate for hydrogen-containing materials or cases where some elements lack quantifiable peaks, because the calculated composition will total less than 100 wt %. Standardless calculations rely on manufacturer-supplied k-ratios and matrix-correction factors derived from elemental standards with similar chemical properties. The excerpt states that calculated accuracies differed between two NPL systems, but does not provide the numerical compositions or error values in the supplied passage; possible causes include spectrum noise, SEM/detector geometry calibration, and peak-area fitting. It contains no evidence on Mg-in-Al or AlSi10Mg minor/trace errors, beam current, count rate, dead time, EBSD indexing, micro-XRF, or ASTM E1508/vendor mechanistic rationale.

## pqac-00000007

From text 'flude2017applicationofbenchtop pages 21-23'.

Stephanie Flude, Michael Haschke, and Michael Storey. Application of benchtop micro-xrf to geological materials. Mineralogical Magazine, 81:923-948, Aug 2017. URL: https://doi.org/10.1180/minmag.2016.080.150, doi:10.1180/minmag.2016.080.150. This article has 191 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides quantitative evidence about benchtop micro-XRF geological-material quantification, but it does not address SEM-EDS, EBSD, LPBF Al-Si alloys, Mg in AlSi10Mg, or acquisition variables such as accelerating voltage, beam current, detector dead time, take-off angle, specimen tilt, exposure time, camera binning, or phase-list choice. For micro-XRF, calibration improves most trace-element results, while major- and minor-element accuracy improves mainly for some standards; accuracy decreases with increasing Fe content, likely because of incorrect assumptions about iron oxidation state and resulting matrix corrections. The authors recommend type-calibration for major/minor elements only when standards have comparable composition and matrix, or when iron oxidation state is known. Without suitable standards, trace-element type-calibration can produce typical relative errors below 100%; the excerpt later states typical errors below 50% for most major/minor elements and up to 100% for most trace elements. With appropriate standards, typical 1σ relative errors may fall below 5% for most major elements and below 6% for some minor elements, although low-abundance P2O5, Na2O, and MgO remain problematic. Relative errors can exceed 100%, yet correspond to absolute errors below 2 wt% for major and 0.2 wt% for minor elements; calibrated trace results are mostly within ±50 ppm. The authors emphasize that benchtop μ-XRF remains less accurate than traditional XRF and cannot substitute for XRF or ICP-MS.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the microstructural evolution and nanomechanical response of additively manufactured AlSi10Mg alloy following T4 (solution treatment + natural ageing) and T6 (solution treatment + artificial ageing) heat treatments. Specimens were fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) and then characterized using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), digital image correlation (DIC), nanoindentation, and surface profilometry. EBSD analysis reveals that solution treatment induces dynamic recrystallization, markedly reducing grain orientation spread (GOS) from 0.58° (as-printed) to < 0.25° (heat-treated), signifying substantial mitigation of SLM-induced residual stresses. Grain refinement follows the trend: as-printed (4.18 μm) > T4 (3.13 μm) > T6 (2.66 μm), consistent with Hall–Petch strengthening (d⁻⁰·⁵). T6 treatment promotes pronounced spheroidization and dissolution of the eutectic Si (silicon) network, precipitate hardening via Mg₂Si formation, and pore coalescence, resulting in superior microstructural homogeneity and ~ 18% lower porosity versus T4. DIC-monitored tensile tests demonstrate a transition from brittle fracture (as-printed, necking absent) to ductile failure with stable necking in heat-treated conditions; T6 exhibits a slightly lower post-necking strain capacity (εₙ = 0.129) compared to T4 (εₙ = 0.131), but demonstrates a higher ultimate tensile strength, indicating a favourable strength–ductility balance. Nanoindentation results reveal a reduction in nanohardness after heat treatment, attributed to dissolution of the as-built eutectic Si network, residual stress relief, precipitate shearing, and improvements in elastic recovery and strain tolerance. The decrease in surface roughness (Ra) from 6.65 μm (as-printed) to 5.29 μm (T6) is attributed to spheroidization of eutectic Si, resulting in a more uniform, less irregular surface morphology. Collectively, these results establish T6 as the optimal post-processing route for enhancing the structural integrity and mechanical reliability of SLM AlSi10Mg components in load-bearing applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Abstract KOBO type extrusion and following cyclic forging in two perpendicular directions at temperatures 150–200 °C were applied to new Mg–9Li–2Al–0.5Sc alloy to study its effect on strength and microstructure evolution. KOBO extrusion of as cast ingot caused significant grain refinement of (α + β) dual phase Mg–9Li–2Al–0.5Sc alloys down to range 1–10 μm for hcp α phase and 1–5 μm for the β phase as resulted from EBSD studies. At that stage ultimate tensile strength UTS of 168 MPa and elongation of 36% were attained. Additional deformation by cyclic forging alternatively from 2 perpendicular directions caused formation of much finer grains of average size of few hundred nm observed using TEM and close to 1 μm applying EBSD technique. Tensile strength increased after that operation above 200 MPa and elongation above 40%, which were the highest observed in the dual phase Mg–Li based alloys. Deformation by cyclic forging induced formation of strong texture with 0001 plane parallel to forging directions. Additional precipitates of size below 1 μm at α/β interfaces or within β phase were identified as hcp AlSc 2 phase. Fine particles of hcp α phase were observed after severe plastic deformation SPD within β phase grains, as effect of diffusion assisted deformation. The amount of hcp α phase increased after SPD up to 70% from initial 40%. High density of defects at α/β interfaces on 0001 planes observed in HRTEM mode was responsible for promotion of hcp phase formation during SPD. Graphic Abstract

Abstract:
We demonstrate the capability of a novel Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) dictionary indexing (DI) approach by means of orientation mapping of a highly deformed graded microstructure in a shot peened Aluminium 7075-T651 alloy. A low microscope accelerating voltage was used to extract, for the first time from a bulk sample, statistically significant orientation information from a region close to a shot crater, showing both recrystallized nano-grains and heavily deformed grains. We show that the robust nature of the DI method allows for faster acquisition of lower quality patterns, limited only by the camera hardware, compared to the acquisition speed and pattern quality required for the conventional Hough indexing (HI) approach. The proposed method paves the way for the quantitative and accurate EBSD characterization of heavily deformed microstructures at a sub-micrometer length scale in cases where the current indexing techniques largely fail.

Abstract:
Better quality control for alloy manufacturing and sorting of post-consumer scraps relies heavily on the accurate determination of their chemical composition. In recent decades, analytical techniques, such as X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (XRF), laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), and spark optical emission spectroscopy (spark-OES), found widespread use in the metal industry, though only a few studies were published about the comparison of these techniques for commercially available alloys. Hence, we conducted a study on the evaluation of four analytical techniques (energy-dispersive XRF, wavelength-dispersive XRF, LIBS, and spark-OES) for the determination of metal sample composition. It focuses on the quantitative analysis of nine commercial alloys, representing the three most important alloy classes: copper, aluminum, and steel. First, spark-OES is proven to serve as a validation technique in the use of certified alloy reference samples. Following an examination of the lateral homogeneity by XRF, the results of the techniques are compared, and reasons for deviations are discussed. Finally, a more general evaluation of each technique with its capabilities and limitations is given, taking operation-relevant parameters, such as measurement speed and calibration effort, into account. This study shall serve as a guide for the routine use of these methods in metal producing and recycling industries.

Abstract:
Abstract Methods within the domain of artificial intelligence are gaining traction for solving a range of materials science objectives, notably the use of deep neural networks for computer vision for the analysis of electron diffraction patterns. An important component of deploying these models is an understanding of the performance as experimental diffraction conditions are varied. This knowledge can inspire confidence in the classifications over a range of operating conditions and identify where performance is degraded. Elucidating the relative impact of each parameter will suggest the most important parameters to vary during the collection of future training data. Knowing which data collection efforts to prioritize is of concern given the time required to collect or simulate vast libraries of diffraction patterns for a wide variety of materials without considering varying any parameters. In this work, five parameters, frame averaging, detector tilt, sample-to-detector distance, accelerating voltage, and pattern resolution, essential to electron diffraction are individually varied during the collection of electron backscatter diffraction patterns to explore the effect on the classifications produced by a deep neural network trained from diffraction patterns captured using a fixed set of parameters. The model is shown to be resilient to nearly all the individual changes examined here.

Abstract:
Abstract The field of metallurgy has greatly benefited from the development of electron microscopy over the last two decades. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) has become a powerful tool for the investigation of nano- and microstructures. This article reviews the complete set of tools for crystallographic analysis in the SEM, i.e., electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD), and electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI). We describe recent relevant developments in electron microscopy, and discuss the state-of-the-art of the techniques and their use for analyses in metallurgy. EBSD orientation measurements provide better angular resolution than spot diffraction in TEM but slightly lower than Kikuchi diffraction in TEM, however, its statistical significance is superior to TEM techniques. Although spatial resolution is slightly lower than in TEM/STEM techniques, EBSD is often a preferred tool for quantitative phase characterization in bulk metals. Moreover, EBSD enables the measurement of lattice strain/rotation at the sub-micron scale, and dislocation density. TKD enables the transmitted electron diffraction analysis of thin-foil specimens. The small interaction volume between the sample and the electron beam enhances considerably the spatial resolution as compared to EBSD, allowing the characterization of ultra-fine-grained metals in the SEM. ECCI is a useful technique to image near-surface lattice defects without the necessity to expose two free surfaces as in TEM. Its relevant contributions to metallography include deformation characterization of metals, including defect visualization, and dislocation density measurements. EBSD and ECCI are mature techniques, still undergoing a continuous expansion in research and industry. Upcoming technical developments in electron sources and optics, as well as detector instrumentation and software, will likely push the border of performance in terms of spatial resolution and acquisition speed. The potential of TKD, combined with EDS, to provide crystallographic, chemical, and morphologic characterizations of nano-structured metals will surely be a valuable asset in metallurgy.

Abstract:
Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) promises to reshape scientific inquiry and enable breakthrough discoveries in areas such as energy storage, quantum computing, and biomedicine. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), a cornerstone of the study of chemical and materials systems, stands to benefit greatly from AI-driven automation. However, present barriers to low-level instrument control, as well as generalizable and interpretable feature detection, make truly automated microscopy impractical. Here, we discuss the design of a closed-loop instrument control platform guided by emerging sparse data analytics. We hypothesize that a centralized controller, informed by machine learning combining limited a priori knowledge and task-based discrimination, could drive on-the-fly experimental decision-making. This platform may unlock practical, automated analysis of a variety of material features, enabling new high-throughput and statistical studies.

This excerpt reports EBSD acquisition settings and a qualitative comparison framework, but it does not provide exact indexing-success percentages, correct-index rates, confidence values, or pattern-quality metrics versus the tested parameters. For shot-peened 7075-T651 aluminum, scans were acquired at 10 kV with 4×4 camera binning and a 25 nm step size. A separate parameter series used 5, 10, and 20 kV at a 120 nm step size, comparing both 4×4 and 8×8 binning. Single-frame averaging, 10 Hough lines at band centers, and 75% Hough resolution were used to simplify indexing and improve speed. The same acquired datasets were indexed using commercial Hough-transform indexing and dictionary indexing, enabling a method comparison independent of acquisition. The authors explicitly state that increasing indexing accuracy generally reduces acquisition speed, but no numerical accuracy-versus-voltage, binning, averaging, beam-current, exposure, or phase-list results are included in this excerpt.
