## 1. seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7 (Context ID: pqac-00000025)

n methods were installed on
                             the system which contains the qualitative classification of main alloys, such as Cu-, Al-, Zn-
                        and steel-base, as well as quantitative calibrations for aluminum and steel. The measurements
                         were performed under room temperature and air conditions, and the MopaLIBS installed over
                          a conveyer belt with tested speeds of 0.5 m/s, 1 m/s, and 2 m/s. The system has a distance
                            sensor to obtain a height profile of the scrap, a cleaning laser, and a LIBS laser. The cleaning
                                    laser, also called pre-ablation laser, cleans the surface of the scraps and has a laser energy of
                          1 mJ, a repetition rate of 100 kHz, a spot size of approximately 100 µm and emits a wavelength
                               of 1064 nm. The properties of the LIBS laser, which is used to generate the plasma, are similar
                               to the pre-ablation laser with one exception: the repetition rate is 20 kHz. The spectrometer is
                           coupled with a CCD-detector and has a wavelength of 240–420 nm, which is covering several
                            atomic emission lines of the target elements. The resolution of the spectrometer is 0.09 nm. The
                         measurement time for one measurement line is ca. 7 ms.Metals 2021, 11, 736                                                                                                            6 of 16





     Figure 3. Schematic drawing of the used MopaLIBS device above a conveyor belt (left). Both the LIBS laser and the
     pre-ablation laser are located behind the distance sensor. The movement direction of the belt is from the left to the right side
     of the image. Microscopic picture of the trace from the pre-ablation laser and shots from the LIBS laser (right).

                         One challenge is the different shapes and heights of individual alloys and scrap pieces.
                             Therefore, a dynamic focusing for an optimal laser alignment is favored, which can be
                          achieved by a distance sensor. It was developed and demonstrated by Bohling et al. that
                             the laser distance sensor of the MopaLIBS allows a dynamic focusing in a range of 140 mm,
                           enabling the investigation of samples with different shapes and heights [21]. With the
                     known sample height proﬁle an optimal laser alignment on the sample surface is assured
                        which provides good spectral data and allows to quantify even minor components.
                              For a robust calibration, partial least squares regression (PLSR) as a multivariate
                       method has been used. At this system, a matrix-speciﬁc calibration for aluminum alloys
                       and steels exists, but unfortunately no calibration for Cu alloys. Accordingly, only the
                             three steels and the three Al test alloys were measured with this LIBS device.

                                   3. Results
                                   3.1. Spark-OES Validation

                              Three steels and three Al alloys were tested to prove the suitability of spark-OES for
                          determining the correct chemical composition. A comparison of the values obtained by
                        two spark-OES with the guaranteed values of the certiﬁed reference alloys (CRAs) is shown
                               in Table 2. The uncertainties of the spark-OES measurements of the CRAs are calculated by
                           using twice the standard deviation, s, and are compared with the certiﬁed absolute errors.
                                 In general, the spark-OES values are in good agreement with certiﬁed values for the
                       CRAs. The absolute deviations of the matrix elements (Al, Fe, Cu) are below 0.3 wt.%
                          with the exception of the ZRM 297-1 sample, for which the Fe content is not certiﬁed and
                      was only calculated to the residue of the sum of all other elements to 100 wt.%. Such a
                          procedure was applied to enable a better visualization of differences between certiﬁed
                       and spark-OES values. However, a fully correct comparison can only be drawn if the
                         Fe content is certiﬁed. For the concentration range from 1 wt.% to 10 wt.%, there are
                           only relative deviations in the elemental composition of less than 5% of the value, though
                             several spark-OES values show higher absolute deviation to the certiﬁed values than
                            the 2s-range of measurement uncertainty. Notable examples are the Cu and Ni contents
                              in different matrices and concentration ranges. The results from the spark-OES for the
                             concentration range below 1 wt.% exhibit that most relative deviations are lower than 10%
                             of the certiﬁed values, exceptions being, for example, Al in the ZRM 192-1 steel or Ni in
                            the BAM-311 Al alloy. Deviations of concentrations in the µg/g-range higher than the
                           corresponding measurement uncertainties cannot be explained by the conﬁned detection
                                limit of the analysis technique itself. Commonly, commercial spark-OES devices are used to
                           determine impurities in the 100 µg/g-range for most elements (with exceptions even in the
                          10 µg/g-range) and show similar or lower quantiﬁcation limits than some of the certiﬁedMetals 2021, 11, 736                                                                                                            7 of 16




                           metal concentrations [22,23]. A reason could be the non-adequate calibration in the lower
                            concentration range for Cu, Ni, Fe, etc. on the devices we employed for this study.

                            referenced alloys for the comparison of analytical techniques is valid because, apart from

RVIEW
When electrons of sufficient energy hit a sample, they generate X-rays of specific energies
characteristic of the elements present. The main challenge of qualitative analysis is to ensure
that all X-ray peaks are detected and correctly labelled as a sample element or a detector
artefact peak. The intensity of the X-ray peaks are not interpreted, although in complex or
noisy spectra, low intensities may cause low concentration elements to be missed. Accurate
qualitative EDX is a prerequisite of any quantitative EDX.


Page 1 of 20NPL Report MAT 135


An example of a periodic table that lists the characteristic X-ray emission energies (Kα, Lα,
and M peaks) for each element can be found at: https://www.edax.com/resources/interactive-
periodic-table. X-ray techniques with higher energy resolution, such as X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS) or SEM wavelength dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-WDS) can split
these into multiple lines (e.g. Kα1, Kα2, Kβ1, etc.), but since the energy resolution of EDX
detectors are usually ≥ 100 eV, only a single broader peak is measured.

Elemental assignment of X-ray peaks might be ambiguous if the peaks from multiple
elements have similar energies (within 30 eV of each other). ISO 22309:2011 Annex B lists
groups of elements with ambiguous X-ray peaks.

Electrons can only generate characteristic X-rays with considerably lower energy than the
primary electron energy. The ratio between the incident electron energy and the
characteristic X-ray energy is called the electron overvoltage. An electron overvoltage of at
least 1.8 is specified for quantitative analysis in ISO 22309:2011. It is not absolutely required
but still recommended for qualitative analysis, as X-ray peaks close to the primary electron
energy may be hidden or very weak. It is impossible to generate X-rays that have a higher
energy than the primary electron energy.

Artefact peaks are not characteristic X-ray peaks of the sample. They need to be identified
and corrected. EDX analysis software packages generally have features built in to do this,
but it is still the operator’s responsibility to check that this has been done correctly and no
peaks have been mislabelled.
Sum peaks (also known as pile-up peaks) happen when two X-ray photons hit the detector
at the same time, and are mistakenly detected as a single X-ray whose energy is the sum of
the two original photons. These appear as small peaks at higher energies that are the sum of
multiple X-ray emission peak energies, e.g. at double the energy of the highest intensity
peak.
Escape peaks are caused by X-ray fluorescence of the detector material, usually made of
silicon, so that the detected X-ray energy is the X-ray emission peak. Escape peaks appear
as small peaks at higher energies, e.g. at double the energy of the highest intensity peak.
The noise peak at near-zero energy is when electronic noise in the detector is mistaken for
near-zero energy photons.

1.2 QUANTITATIVE EDX METHOD OVERVIEW
EDX quantification is based on the principle that X-ray peak intensities for an element
increase with concentration of that element in a sample. However, there are two problems:
   (1) X-ray detector efficiency is not constant, so identical X-ray intensities hitting the EDX
      detector at, for example, 1 keV and 8 keV will not lead to identical peak areas at 1 keV
     and 8 keV; and
   (2) the generated characteristic X-ray intensities are not linear with concentration, so
     doubling the atomic concentration of an element does not necessarily double the
      intensity of characteristic X-rays hitting the EDX detector.

All quantitative analysis considers the characteristic X-ray peaks only, which means it is
necessary to remove the intensity contribution of background X-rays generated by
Brehmsstralung radiation. Background correction is important in quantification, but different
EDX analysis software packages use different methods and this usually cannot be tuned by
the user. However, a poor background fit (Figure 1b), which leads to inadequate peak area
determination, is still a useful warning sign to the operator that that the quantitative results
have high uncertainty.




Page 2 of 20NPL Report MAT 135



              (a)





              (b)





      Figure 1: Example spectra with (a) good and (b) bad background fit.

Problem (1) explains why elemental standards are needed for full quantitative analysis, so
that differences in detector efficiency can be cancelled out. The detector window material
affects detector efficiency, especially in the low X-ray energy range (see Figure 9 in [5]).
Beryllium windows absorb the majority of X-rays below 1 keV and therefore are not suitable
for use with low-Z elements below Na (Na K = 1.04 keV). Si3N4 or polymer thin windows
perform better, but the efficiency drops off significantly and is discontinuous in this energy
range. Windowless detectors would be preferable but are not currently available at NPL in
2024. Contamination buildup in the SEM can also affect efficiency for all detector
configurations.

Problem (2) is why background subtraction and matrix corrections are needed (also known
as ZAF corrections: Z = atomic number, A = X-ray absorption, F = X-ray fluorescence).
These account for the effects of:
 -   Electron backscattering (which increases with atomic number Z), where incoming
    electrons are either scattered back out of the sample without generating an X-ray, and
    electron stopping power, which describes how electrons lose energy (and the
    corresponding ability to excite atoms and generate X-rays) as they penetrate the sample.
 -   X-ray Absorption, which means that X-rays generated by the sample are absorbed
    before they leave the sample and never make it to the detector.
 -  Secondary X-ray Fluorescence, which means that high-energy X-rays generated in the
    sample generate lower-energy X-rays. As a result, the high-energy X-ray is not detected,
    but extra low-energy X-rays are detected by EDX.


Page 3 of 20NPL Report MAT 135


The theory relating to ZAF matrix corrections are more naturally described by weight
fractions instead of atomic fractions. This is why EDX compositions are calculated as
weight % even though the k-ratios are more naturally expressed in atom %.

Not every X-ray line is in the standards database, so for example the Fe-L peaks (0.705 keV)
may not be used for quantification if only the Fe-K peaks (6.403 keV) are included in the
database. This must then be taken into account when selecting SEM accelerating voltage –
for example, the Fe-K peak requires at least 12 kV electron energy to be adequately excited
for quantitative analysis.

ABSTRACT
Fully quantitative elemental composition measurements using energy dispersive X-ray
spectroscopy in a scanning electron microscope (SEM-EDX) are only possible for elements
with an atomic number of at least 11, in samples which meet stringent requirements, and
where elemental standards of well-known composition and similar chemistry are available. In
practice, is often not possible to meet these criteria and low atomic number samples are
increasingly requiring analysis; in these cases, qualitative or semi-quantitative EDX results
can still be useful. This report describes the detector and system checks and corresponding
measurement uncertainties using both conventional standards and a low atomic number
ionic liquid standard containing only light elements with well-known composition. Example
use cases for quantitative, semi-quantitative and qualitative EDX measurements are
described and lower bound uncertainties estimated. A decision tree is provided to guide good
practice in experimental approach and data analysis.NPL Report MAT 135

1  INTRODUCTION

Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy in a scanning electron microscope (SEM-EDX or
SEM-EDS – the terms are generally used interchangeably) can be used to characterise
elemental compositions with a spatial resolution of around 1 – 5 μm.

EDX can be quantitative or qualitative. Qualitative EDX analysis is the most flexible and has
fewest requirements. Fully quantitative EDX has stringent experimental constraints and
requires elemental standards, but can measure elemental compositions with ± 5 % relative
uncertainty. Standardless analysis methods are often described as ‘semi-quantitative’; they
are more flexible in terms of experimental requirements but the uncertainties are greater at
up to ± 30 % relative uncertainty, and in the case of normalised standardless analysis, large
errors may be hidden in a plausible output value [1], [2].

International Standards covering analysis and quantification by EDX include ISO 15632:2021
[3] which covers measurement of the EDX spectrometer efficiency and resolution, and
ISO 22309:2011 [4] which describes how to perform quantitative EDX, specifically limited to
elements with atomic numbers (Z) > 11 (Na and above).

Light element quantification by EDX has greater uncertainty and additional uncertainty
sources, such as increased X-ray absorption within the sample, particularly if higher-Z
elements are also present, and increased sensitivity to surface topography [5]. This is why
the quantitative analysis procedure in ISO 22309:2011 is considered applicable only for
elements with Z > 11. However, the commercial need for EDX measurements is increasing
for low-Z materials such as battery electrodes (carbon), organic materials (carbon, nitrogen,
oxygen), and semiconductor devices (silicon).

Therefore, this report looks specifically at quantitative EDX measurements and uncertainties
of an ionic liquid, a low-Z standard material with known composition, to provide lower-bound
uncertainty values for what to expect with quantitative EDX on low-Z materials. To put these
values into context, the report also describes qualitative measurements on a low atomic
number sample, and quantitative and semi-quantitative measurements on a Fe/Cr/Ni certified
reference material i.e. a much higher atomic number based sample.

The remainder of this section briefly considers the background to the requirements for
qualitative, semi-quantitative and quantitative analysis. Figure 2 then lays out, in a decision
tree format, which EDX analysis methods are possible for different use cases. Section 2
describes the samples used in this report and gives examples of experimental acquisition of
datasets using two different EDX systems, called in this report System A and System B.
Section 3 then provides analysis of data sets and composition uncertainties for each analysis
method. The results are shown without attribution to the different detector systems as
samples were not necessarily analysed under identical conditions, or by both systems, so
comparisons would not be appropriate. Appendix 1 lists the specifications of the NPL EDX
systems used in this report.

1.1 QUALITATIVE EDX METHOD OVERVIEW
When electrons of sufficient energy hit a sample, they generate X-rays of specific energies
characteristic of the elements present. The main challenge of qualitative analysis is to ensure
that all X-ray peaks are detected and correctly labelled as a sample element or a detector
artefact peak. The intensity of the X-ray peaks are not interpreted, although in complex or
noisy spectra, low intensities may cause low concentration elements to be missed. Accurate
qualitative EDX is a prerequisite of any quantitative EDX.

3.3 SEMI-QUANTITATIVE – UNNORMALISED STANDARDLESS ANALYSIS
The experimental procedure is more complicated, but is more conservative since errors tend
to appear as total concentrations that do not add up to 100 wt %. Therefore, it is required for
samples that may contain unknown (trace) elements or hydrogen, where normalised analysis
would hide these errors by forcing the total to 100 wt %. This is available only with one of the
two systems.

An additional spectrum from a pure element standard such as Co is acquired at the same
sample position and beam current as the sample X-ray spectra. The sample preparation
requirements are identical to normalised standardless analysis. This is used to normalise the
EDX detector geometry and electron beam current with respect to the factory-supplied X-ray
peak intensities values. Therefore, the beam current must be stable over the duration of the
experiment.

       2.2.3.2 Detection of Diffraction Bands

       Once EBSPs have been transformed into the Hough space, the calculation of
the indexing and intensity responses can be achieved.  First, to help the automatic

                                                                        18detection of peaks (diffraction bands) by EBSD systems, a convolution mask  is
applied to Hough images. This mask has a butterfly-like shape, which is similar to the
one of Hough peaks (see Figure 7) [32, 33]. The use of this kind of mask helps to
remove the noise in Hough images, which improves the contrast of Hough peaks
(contrast between minimum and maximum  intensities of each peak) and  their
automatic detection by EBSD systems. Indeed, peak detection algorithms look for
maximum or minimum peak intensities in Hough images (in other words, it looks for
center or edges of diffraction bands). To obtain the best results (good contrast of
Hough peaks and precise peak detection), the width of the butterfly mask should be
adjusted  for each Hough peak of a Hough  image.  Indeed,  for  a given SEM
accelerating  voltage,  the  width  of  diffraction  bands  varies  according  to  the
crystallographic planes (bands) considered and to the position of these planes (bands)
in an EBSP (see section 2.2.2.1). Consequently, the width of Hough peaks varies in a
Hough image, so the importance of adjusting the butterfly mask for each peak of a
Hough image (to get the best fit between the mask and each Hough peak). However,
in practice, the size of a butterfly mask is fixed for all peaks of a same Hough image.
While this situation is generally adequate for most geometrical analyses ofEBSPs (i.e.
indexing response of EBSD systems), this may become a real issue for analyses of
EBSPs based on intensity data (e.g. intensity response, see section 2.3).

(peak) detection algorithms were developed for the indexing response of EBSD
systems, not for assessing any EBSP contrast or diffraction band intensities. For
example, besides its automatic character for band detection, the Hough transform was
chosen among other mathematical or image analysis techniques because it improves
the indexing accuracy of EBSPs (accuracy in band or peak detection). Indeed, one
property of the Hough transform is that  it is only slightly affected by the noise in
images and so, by a loss in the EBSP quality (the Hough transform is effective for
indexing blurred EBSPs) [16, 17]. Therefore, the Hough transform and similarly the
EBSP processing steps associated with band detection may not be the most suitable or
optimal ones for calculating an EBSD response (e.g. the intensity response) based on
intensity data of EBSPs rather than geometrical data.

2.3.4  Strain Analyses

       With the indexing response of EBSD systems, each EBSD data point  is
associated with one value of crystal orientation. For strain analysis purposes, the
EBSD user can then correlate  this value with a specific type of twins or grain
boundaries, or this value can be used to calculate different strain parameters including
Taylor and Schmid  factors. With a good understanding of the EBSD technique
(system  calibration and sources of uncertainties),  precise and quantitative  strain
analyses can be performed with the indexing response of EBSD systems, which is not
the case of strain analyses achieved with the current intensity response of EBSD
systems. Indeed, strain analyses (or any microstructural analysis) with the intensity
response  are  generally performed by observing grey-tone  variations  in  intensity


                                                                      23tmages and by making correlations with the expected microstructure or the one
observed with indexing results or other characterization techniques. However, because
the EBSP quality and the intensity response are influenced by several experimental
conditions (see section 2.3.3), it is actually not possible to relate a specific grey-tone
to one type of strain mechanisms (crystal defects) or to a specific level of strain in a
material. Moreover,  as mentioned  section  2.2, exact properties of the  intensity
response of unknown  (e.g.  strain sensitivity, reproducibility, effects of the EBSP
processing steps). Consequently, only qualitative or semi-quantitative strain analyses
can actually be performed with the intensity response of EBSD systems.
       Very few authors have  tried to understand and to develop the  intensity
response of commercial EBSD systems  for  strain analyses of materials.  In  this
connection, Tucker et al. (2000) mentioned in a paper that commercial EBSD systems
"have tended to adopt only simple measures of pattern quality (intensity response),
presumably  in  order  to maximize  the  speed of orientation mapping  (indexing
response) which is seen as the primary use of the EBSD technique" [38]. On the other
hand, this situation may also be explained by the fact that EBSD technologies were
not appropriate in the 90s for achieving strain analyses based on the EBSP quality.
Indeed, until then, the resolution and sensitivity of EBSD cameras were not enough
advanced for acquiring good EBSP quality and/or for capturing slight changes in the
EBSP quality caused by the presence of strain in materials. Additionally, a lower
computer memory space may also explain the development of one EBSP processing
procedure rather than two (e.g. one for the indexing response and one for the intensity
response).
       Mackenzie et Dingley (1987) and Quested et al. (1988) were the first authors
to propose the use and quantification of the EBSP quality (then called pattern
diffuseness) as a mean for assessing dislocation contents in materials [39,40]. Indeed,
these authors showed that the visual aspect of EBSPs deteriorates when the strain
level of materials increased. Moreover, Mackenzie et Dingley found that the EBSP
quality could be well analysed by looking to frequency intensity variations in EBSPs
previously transformed into the Fourier space. Indeed, they showed that EBSPs of
high quality (un strained materials) show more high frequency intensity variations than
EBSPs of lower quality (deformed materials). Some years later, this F ourier approach
was reconsidered by Wilkinson et Dingley, who quantified the EBSP quality (pattern
diffuseness) by calculating the spectral first peak area (SFP A) and the power spectra

                                                                   24first moment (PSFM) of specific EBSP zone axes (e.g. <112»  [3]. These authors
found that these parameters (SFP A and PSFM) varied approximately linearly with the
amount of strain in a material (for a 6061 aluminum alloy).
        However, one major disadvantage of the previously-described techniques is
that they had to be performed manually and were thus time-consuming. Indeed, each
EBSP had to be recorded on a photographic film and then digitised before achieving
any strain analysis. Consequently, these techniques were not suitable for automatic
EBSD mapping. Today, with the emergence of new EBSD cameras and greater
computer memory space, Fourier image analysis techniques (and other image analysis
techniques) could be revisited and (quantitatively) compared to the current intensity
response of commercial EBSD  systems. Moreover,  these comparisons could be
extended to other definitions of the intensity response such as those studied by Tao
(2003) and Wright (2006) and which are based on Hough images of EBSPs (e.g.:
intensity mean, deviation and entropy of Hough images) [9,41].

A method was developed to calculate the characteristic X ray intensities from a paint bilayer
structure containing two layers of a mixture of commonly used white paints (ZnO, PbO,
BaSO4, TiO2). For Ti and Zn the Kα and Kβ lines, for Pb the Lα and Lβ lines, and for Ba the
Ll, Lα, Lβ1, Lβ2, Lγ1 and Lγ2,3 lines are incorporated. The model can easily be extended to
further materials and X ray lines. The method was applied for a system composed of ZnO and
PbO. X ray spectra taken from several paintings have shown the simultaneous presence of
these paints. The important question is immediately raised whether the paints were mixed
together or painted one over another. Taking into account that the energy dependent X ray
attenuation is different in the two cases, the measurement of the relative line intensities could
provide information in this respect. In the particular situation where an infinitely thick PbO
layer is covered by a ZnO layer of increasing thickness, our calculation shows that in the case
of mixing no change can be expected in the Pb–Lβ/Pb–Lα ratio. If the ZnO layer is painted
onto the PbO layer, on the other hand, this ratio is rapidly increasing, as displayed in Fig. 20.
The very interesting fact that this relative line intensity is constant in the case of mixture is
due to a lucky accident: the ratios of the mass attenuation coefficients for the Pb–Lα and Pb–
Lβ in PbO and ZnO are practically the same.

3.5. Dosimetric tests

The non-destructiveness of the method is based on the fact that the energy transferred is too
negligible to cause any damage. But even the mention of any chance of a radiation hazard, on
the other hand, is a rather inhibiting factor for allowing the spectrometer to enter a public
collection. In order to gain reassuring information, the radiation dose around the source-
detector assembly was checked in two ways. Using a hand-held dosimeter, measurements
were made around the analysed spot at different distances. Figure 21 shows the result of a
measurement in the vicinity of the 109Cd excitation head. The dosimeter indicates 8 µSv/h.
Taking into account the radiation shielding of the radioactive sources, no significant dose was
expected, and these rough tests have confirmed the expectations. In addition, long term dose
measurements were also carried out using a fixed arrangement of TTL tablets. Ten tablets
were put onto a wooden stick grid around the excitation head (Fig. 22.) and exposed to the
radiation for 5 days for both the 109Cd and 241Am sources. The highest value obtained was
about 13 µSv/h. The dose rate level at distances longer than 20 cm was below the detection
limit.

3.6. Miscellaneous

Our  laboratory  took  part  in  the  Proficiency  Test  Exercise  for XRF  Laboratories
(PTXRFIAEA/01) organized by the IAEA. We also participated in the GeoPT International
proficiency test organized by Dr. Phil Potts. The evaluation of the test run is ongoing.


1324. Summary

The work within the frame and with financial support of the CRP has essentially followed the
intentions of the detailed plan. A rather versatile portable XRF spectrometer with radioisotope
excitation was built. The heart of the spectrometer is an AMPTEK XR-100CR X ray detector
together with the matching PXT/CR power supply and amplifier. Compact excitation heads
containing 55Fe, 109Cd and 241Am radiation can be alternatively used to cover the widest
elemental range. The system was applied for real in situ analysis of paint layers. Taking into
account that the samples to be analysed were unique precious samples, sample preparation
and calibration processes for general use could not be specified in this particular application
of the in situ use of XRF. Instead of more or less useless efforts to make general calibrations,
our work was focused on contributing to the solution of the important practical problem when
Ti (Ti white) has to be detected or its presence excluded. A calculation method was also
developed in order to gain information from the relative X ray line intensity. Mainly due to
administrative difficulties, the planned pilot studies in a public collection had to be postponed
and it was not possible to carry out the planned measurements on painted stone archaeological
objects. Instead of these measurements, interesting applications were found with the help of
private art collectors, and solution of the problems they requested fitted very well into the
main intentions of our participation in the CRP.

Abstract

Portable energy-dispersive X ray fluorescence equipment, mainly composed of a small sized X ray tube and
thermoelectrically cooled X ray detector, were employed to analyse paintings. The frescos of Giotto in the
chapel of the Scrovegni in Padua were analysed, and oil paintings by De Chirico, of which 15 of certain
attribution, and 11 supposedly painted by De Chirico. The pollution effects on the Giotto frescos were
determined by analysing sulphur on the surface, and the thickness and composition of golden haloes were also
measured. The 11 oil paintings by De Chirico are possibly fakes, on the basis of the different fingerprints of
authentified and unauthentified paintings.

1. Introduction

Energy dispersive X ray fluorescence (EDXRF) analysis is a non destructive, multielemental
and simple technique which is based on irradiation of a sample by a low intensity X ray beam,
and on detection of secondary X rays emitted by the sample. The energy of these secondary
X rays is characteristic of the elements present in the sample, and the intensity is proportional
to their concentration. The thickness of the sample involved in the analysis depends on the
element, on the matrix and on the energy of the primary and secondary radiation.

The typical portable equipment for EDXRF analysis is composed basically of an X ray tube,
an X ray detector with related electronics and a multichannel analyser.

EDXRF systems are very useful for analysis of works of art, because the analysis is non-
destructive, multielemental, simple and relatively inexpensive. Portability of the systems is
almost mandatory. In fact, in very few cases it is possible to study a work of art outside its
normal location (museum, church, excavation, etc.).

There are many materials as well as a variety of problems in archaeometry that can be studied
by using an EDXRF apparatus. There are then cases in which a qualitative or a semi-
quantitative analysis is sufficient (for example in the case of paintings); in this case it is more
important to know the relative amount of an element in different points of the surface and/or
at different depths, than to quantitatively determine the chemical elements.

Recently developed thermoelectrically cooled semiconductor detectors, such as Si-PIN, Si-
drift, CdZnTe, CdTe and HgI2, coupled to miniaturized low-power, dedicated X ray tubes, are
well suited for assembling portable systems for EDXRF analysis of archaeological samples.

In this paper, EDXRF analysis of Giotto’s frescos in the Chapel of the Scrovegni in Padua is
described, as well as that of 26 oil paintings by De Chirico or ascribed to De Chirico.





                                                                                1512. Instrumentation

A typical portable EDXRF system is mainly composed of:

•  an X ray tube,
•  an X ray detector with electronics,
•  a multi-channel analyser.

2.1. X ray tubes

A great variety of X ray tubes of various types (anode, maximum voltage, current), size and
cost are currently available for EDXRF analysis, depending on the problem, and more
specifically on the element or elements, to be analysed. Low-power X ray tubes with selected
anodes are generally adequate. They may be chosen primarily as a function of the atomic
number of the elements to be analysed. Table I gives a survey of useful portable X ray tubes
[1–2].

A small sized, low power W-anode X ray tube working up to 40 kV, 0.1 mA, is adequate for
analysis of almost all elements of archaeometric interest. Working at low voltages (5–10 kV)
or at high voltages (35–40 kV), this tube is able to excite low atomic number elements such as
S and Cl, or elements from Ca to Pb, respectively [2] (Fig. 1).

2.2. X ray detectors [3]

In the last few years, small sized thermoelectrically cooled semiconductor detectors have
become available, such as Si-PIN [3], Si-drift [4], CZT [3-5], CdTe [3–6] and HgI2 [7–8].

These detectors are cooled to about –30°C by means of a Peltier circuit, and are contained in
small sized boxes also including a high quality preamplifier and the Peltier circuit.

HgI2 detectors were the first to be constructed and have currently an energy resolution of
about 180–200 eV at 5.9 keV, and an efficiency of about 100% in the whole range of X rays.

Si-PIN detectors, with an Si thickness of 300–500 µm, exhibit an energy resolution of 160–
200 eV, and are useful up to about 25 keV because of the decreasing efficiency versus energy,
due to the limited thickness. Because of the high shaping time of the amplifier (12 µm) these
detectors are also not convenient for high counting rates.




154Si-drift detectors have an Si thickness of 300 µm and an energy resolution of about 140–
150 eV at 5.9 keV. They are able to work also at high counting rates.

CZT detectors have a typical thickness of 2 mm and an efficiency of about 100% in the whole
X ray range. The energy resolution is about 300 and 700 eV at 5.9 and 59.6 keV, respectively.

3. Theoretical background

A painting may be considered as a succession of pigment layers. In a fresco, over the plaster
there is a preparation layer, and then one or more pigment layers. In an oil painting, over the
canvas there  is a preparation layer, and then, again, one or more pigment layers. The
penetration of incident and output radiation is determined by exponential laws of the type e
(–µx), where the exponent is depending on the attenuation coefficient of the single layer at
incident and output radiation, multiplied by the thickness of the layer. The thickness of a
pigment layer is generally very low, and therefore the exponential may be reduced to (1 – µx).

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a compact proposal-ready evidence table with columns: technique/acquisition choice, quantitative fidelity effect, interpretation for metal-alloy microanalysis, and source context IDs. Include SEM-EDS standards \u00b15% vs standardless up to \u00b130%; overvoltage >=1.8 and 35\u00b0 detector geometry; dead time 10\u201320%; standardless and standards-based NIST alloy errors; EBSD scan-speed indexing rates 54 vs 154 PPS, frame averaging 1/5/10/20/30 and sixfold speed gain, 10/20/30 kV, resolutions, phase-list zero-correct case; micro-XRF 15\u201350 kV, 12\u2013106 \u00b5A and filter thicknesses, 10\u2013100 ppm MDLs, and Mg Al-alloy errors of 40% and 5000%. Clearly label where evidence is transferable rather than LPBF AlSi10Mg-specific."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Technique/acquisition choice | Quantitative fidelity effect | Interpretation for metal-alloy microanalysis | Source context IDs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SEM-EDS: standards-based vs standardless** | Physical standards can support about **±5% relative uncertainty**; standardless analysis can reach **±30%**, and normalization to 100% can conceal errors. | Standards are needed for qualification-grade alloy chemistry; standardless results should be treated as semi-quantitative. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020) |
| **SEM-EDS: accelerating voltage/overvoltage** | ISO 22309 specifies incident energy of at least **1.8× the selected X-ray-line energy**; adequate Fe-K excitation, for example, requires at least **12 kV**. Measurements at **5, 10, and 20 kV** produced substantial composition scatter in a low-energy-line test material. | Voltage determines excitation efficiency and interaction volume; one fixed voltage is not valid for every alloying element. | (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) |
| **SEM-EDS: take-off geometry** | Quantitative protocols require a flat surface normal to the beam and approximately **35° to the EDS detector**. Low take-off angles at holes and grooves reduced integral counts and the number of detected elements. | Tilt, roughness, pores, and melt-pool relief can create element-dependent absorption errors, especially for low-energy Mg and Al lines. | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000019) |
| **SEM-EDS: beam current/dead time** | Beam current and dead time were identified as dominant variables; **10–20% dead time** was recommended. In standards-based work, beam-current drift was held to **0.2%** over a **20 min** session. | Too little current gives poor counting statistics, while excessive rate causes pile-up and dead-time losses; current must be measured or controlled. | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000020) |
| **SEM-EDS: normalized standardless NIST Fe-Cr-Ni alloy** | At **20 kV**, errors were **+1.3% Cr, −0.4% Fe, and −0.8% Ni**; on another system at **25 kV**, they were **−3.1%, +1.3%, and −4.1%**. | Even favorable major-element results vary with detector calibration, fitting, matrix corrections, and factory databases. | (pqac-00000019) |
| **SEM-EDS: unnormalized standardless vs standards** | Unnormalized standardless analysis gave **−0.7% Cr, −2.3% Fe, and −2.7% Ni** and totaled **98.1 wt%**. Physical standards reduced errors to **<1%** against NIST EDS values, although residual uncertainty versus wet chemistry was **3–7%** because of ZAF corrections. | Standards cancel much of the beam-current, geometry, detector-efficiency, and contamination dependence, but matrix-correction uncertainty remains. | (pqac-00000020) |
| **SEM-EDS: Mg in LPBF AlSi10Mg** | **Evidence gap:** no controlled SEM-EDS parameter sweep for minor Mg in LPBF AlSi10Mg was found. General evidence places standardless uncertainty as high as **±30%**, with greater risk for low-energy/light-element peaks. | Apparent Mg differences in AlSi10Mg cannot reliably be assigned to metallurgy without alloy- and instrument-specific validation. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020) |
| **EBSD: scan speed—transferable metal evidence** | Increasing speed from **54 to 154 patterns/s** reduced conventional indexing success from **34.9% to 9.3%**. At 54 patterns/s, processing raised success to **41.3–59.7%**; at 154 patterns/s, improved values reached approximately **12.5–37.6%**. | Faster mapping can turn most pixels into non-indexed or unreliable measurements and make grain statistics cleanup-dependent. | (pqac-00000009) |
| **EBSD: frame averaging/exposure—transferable metal evidence** | Tests used **1, 5, 10, 20, and 30 frames**. One-frame patterns were almost entirely misclassified; improvement began at five, reasonable classification appeared at ten, and nearly all patterns were correct at 20–30. Five instead of 30 frames yielded a **6× speed gain** with high accuracy for most phases. | Exposure must be optimized against throughput rather than minimized; map appearance alone does not establish fidelity. | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| **EBSD: accelerating voltage—transferable metal evidence** | At **10, 20, and 30 kV**, 10 kV caused many misclassifications, 20 kV was the default, and 30 kV gave reasonably good performance. | Lower voltage can improve spatial resolution but reduce indexing reliability unless current, exposure, and indexing are re-optimized. | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| **EBSD: resolution/binning—transferable Al evidence** | Al 7075 was mapped at **5, 10, and 20 kV** using **4×4 and 8×8 binning**. Another study tested **156×128, 622×512, and 1244×1024** patterns; low resolution retained high accuracy for most phases but affected similar structures more strongly. | Binning accelerates acquisition but removes diffraction detail; suitability is phase- and microstructure-dependent. | (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| **EBSD: phase-list selection—transferable duplex-alloy evidence** | With two correct phases, Hough indexing produced a high-fidelity map. Expanding the list to **12 candidates** caused **zero patterns** to index as either correct phase despite ideal acquisition settings. | Phase-list choice can overwhelm improvements in beam conditions and generate confident but false phase maps. | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) |
| **EBSD: LPBF Al-Si-specific evidence** | **Evidence gap:** retrieved LPBF AlSi10Mg studies did not provide controlled factorial data for indexing rate or confidence versus current, voltage, exposure, binning, and phase list. | Published settings are examples, not validated optima; systematic LPBF Al-Si acquisition-response data are needed. | (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016) |
| **Micro-XRF: voltage/current/filters** | A commercial alloy protocol used **15–50 kV**, **12–106 µA**, and automatic filters of **75 µm Cu/25 µm Ti/200 µm Al**, **38 µm Al**, **25 µm Ti/300 µm Al**, or **25 µm Fe**. A **60 s** measurement comprised separate **30 s** light- and heavy-element scans. | Excitation must be element- and matrix-specific; a high-voltage transition-metal setting is not automatically sensitive to Mg, Al, or Si. | (pqac-00000028) |
| **Micro-XRF: current, optics, and filter sensitivity** | Tests used **40 kV/0.2 mA**, increased current from **0.2 to 1.0 mA** on Ag-Cu alloy, and evaluated **12.5–50 µm Mo** and **50–200 µm Al** filters. Polycapillary spectra were **35–40×** more intense than monocapillary spectra, with flux-density gain up to approximately **300×**. | Current controls photon statistics until rate limits intervene; filters and optics reshape both background and elemental sensitivity. | (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022) |
| **Micro-XRF: detection limits** | At **40 kV/0.2 mA** and **1000 s**, minimum detection limits were typically **10–100 ppm**; examples included **23–68 ppm Mn**, **10–22 ppm Rb**, and **68–94 ppm Ca**, depending on tube and optics. | Trace sensitivity cannot be transferred between instruments without documenting tube, optics, filter, atmosphere, detector, and live time. | (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022) |
| **Micro-XRF: matrix correction/calibration** | With suitable matrix-matched calibration, typical errors can fall below **5% for major** and **6% for some minor elements**. Without suitable standards, errors were typically below **50% for major/minor** and up to **100% for trace elements**, with some exceeding 100%. | Fundamental-parameter corrections do not remove matrix dependence; alloy-specific reference materials remain necessary. | (pqac-00000007) |
| **XRF: Mg errors in Al alloys—transferable to AlSi10Mg risk** | In AlMg4.5Mn0.7, EDXRF over-reported Mg by about **2 wt%**, approximately **40% relative**. In nominal Al99.5, it reported **0.196 wt% instead of 0.004 wt%**, a **5000% relative deviation**. | Minor/trace Mg can be grossly biased in commercial alloy modes. These cases are XRF—not SEM-EDS—and are not LPBF-specific, but quantify the light-element risk in Al matrices. | (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029) |
| **Expertise dependence and sparse rationale** | Operators remain responsible for checking artefact peaks and background fits. EBSD quality definitions are vendor-specific and partly documented; parameter effects remain incompletely quantified. Manufacturer-constrained software prevented investigators from identifying why two systems produced different standardless accuracies. | Standards and vendor defaults provide thresholds and operating envelopes, but not transparent alloy-specific response models; optimization remains instrument-, specimen-, and operator-dependent. | (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) |


*Table: Proposal-ready quantitative evidence linking SEM-EDS, EBSD, and micro-XRF acquisition choices to measurement fidelity in metal alloys. Transferable evidence and the absence of controlled LPBF AlSi10Mg parameter studies are explicitly identified.*

{"answer": "# Quantitative evidence for a funding-proposal needs statement

## Executive conclusion

Acquisition settings are not merely operational details: they determine whether SEM-EDS returns approximately quantitative chemistry or a normalized but biased composition, whether EBSD maps contain mostly correct orientations or mostly failed/misassigned pixels, and whether micro-XRF detects minor alloying additions or overestimates them by orders of magnitude. The literature supports a strong need for **alloy-, instrument-, and task-specific acquisition-response models**, especially for LPBF Al-Si-Mg, because controlled factorial studies connecting settings to ground-truth fidelity are sparse.

The key quantitative evidence is summarized below.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 1. SEM-EDS quantification

### Standards-based versus standardless accuracy

An NPL uncertainty assessment states that fully quantitative SEM-EDS under stringent conditions and with physical standards can achieve approximately **±5% relative uncertainty**, whereas standardless methods can have uncertainty as high as **±30%**. Normalized standardless analysis is particularly hazardous because forcing the reported total to 100 wt% can hide missing elements or large errors behind a plausible-looking result (pqac-00000018).

For a NIST Fe-Cr-Ni reference alloy, normalized standardless analysis at **20 kV** gave errors of **+1.3% Cr, −0.4% Fe, and −0.8% Ni** on one system. A second system at **25 kV** gave **−3.1% Cr, +1.3% Fe, and −4.1% Ni**. The investigators could not determine why the systems differed because detector hardware, analysis algorithms, geometry calibration, peak fitting, matrix corrections, and remote standards databases were manufacturer-constrained (pqac-00000019).

Unnormalized standardless analysis of the same alloy gave relative errors of **−0.7% Cr, −2.3% Fe, and −2.7% Ni**, with a visibly deficient total of **98.1 wt%**. Physical pure-element standards reduced errors to **<1% relative to NIST EDS values**, although residual disagreement with wet chemistry remained **3–7%**, attributed to ZAF matrix corrections. Standards measured in the same session cancel much of the dependence on beam current, detector geometry, contamination, and detector efficiency (pqac-00000020).

### Accelerating voltage

ISO 22309 specifies an electron overvoltage of at least **1.8**, meaning incident energy should be at least 1.8 times the energy of every X-ray line used quantitatively. For example, adequate Fe-K excitation requires at least approximately **12 kV**. Voltage therefore cannot be selected solely for spatial resolution: it determines whether a line is efficiently excited and also changes interaction volume and absorption (pqac-00000017).

The dependence is experimentally visible. Standardless measurements of the same light-element material at **5, 10, and 20 kV** produced large between-voltage scatter; pooled results had errors of **−19% C, −31% N, +2.8% O, +15% F, and +3.4% S**. Although this is not an alloy, it demonstrates the pronounced voltage sensitivity of low-energy lines relevant to Mg and Al analysis (pqac-00000019).

### Beam current, count rate, and dead time

Beam current increases X-ray counts and reduces counting uncertainty, but high input rates increase dead time, pulse pile-up, and sum peaks. One parameter-optimization study identified beam current/intensity and dead time as the variables exerting the greatest influence on EDS results and recommended operating at **10–20% dead time** (pqac-00000002).

For rigorous standards-based analysis, the NPL reference-alloy experiment limited measured beam-current drift to **0.2%** over a **20 min** acquisition session. Unnormalized standardless analysis likewise requires a stable current because a separately acquired reference spectrum normalizes current and detector geometry. Ratio-based methods that derive elemental ratios within the same spectrum can suppress current instability and have reported accuracy better than **5%**, but their calibration factors remain beam-energy dependent (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000020).

### Take-off geometry and specimen topography

The quantitative protocol requires a flat, polished surface normal to the beam and approximately **35° to the EDS detector**. In practical tests, holes and grooves substantially changed integrated counts and even the number of elements identified because low local take-off angles obstructed emitted X-rays (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000019). This is directly relevant to LPBF alloys: pores, melt-pool relief, incompletely polished Si particles, and tilted surfaces preferentially absorb low-energy Mg and Al X-rays.

### Minor/trace Mg in aluminum

The retrieved literature did **not** provide a controlled SEM-EDS parameter sweep for Mg in LPBF AlSi10Mg against certified bulk chemistry. That absence is itself an important proposal gap. The strongest defensible SEM-EDS statement is that standardless errors can reach **±30%**, light-element uncertainty is greater, and normalized output can conceal missing mass (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020).

Closely analogous XRF alloy evidence shows how severe the Al-matrix/light-element problem can become: Mg in AlMg4.5Mn0.7 was over-reported by approximately **2 wt%**, or **40% relative**, while nominal Al99.5 was reported as **0.196 wt% Mg instead of 0.004 wt%**, a **5000% relative deviation**. These are XRF rather than SEM-EDS results and must not be presented as SEM-EDS performance, but they quantitatively demonstrate why trace Mg in an Al matrix requires matrix-matched validation rather than reliance on an automatic alloy mode (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029).

## 2. EBSD indexing and confidence

### Beam current and exposure

Beam current and exposure jointly determine electron dose and pattern signal-to-noise ratio. Direct current sweeps were not recovered for LPBF AlSi10Mg, but controlled frame-averaging data quantify the dose/throughput tradeoff. A study varied averaging among **1, 5, 10, 20, and 30 frames** over **3,848 patterns** in a duplex alloy. At one frame, essentially all patterns were misclassified; five improved the result, ten produced a reasonable fraction of correct classifications, and 20–30 produced nearly complete agreement with the reference phase map. Reducing averaging from 30 to five made acquisition **six times faster** while retaining high accuracy for most tested phases, but the most crystallographically similar phases remained vulnerable (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

Independent conventional-indexing data show the consequence of faster acquisition. Increasing collection rate from **54 to 154 patterns/s** reduced correctly indexed patterns from **34.9% to 9.3%**. At 54 patterns/s, rescanning or neighbor-based processing increased success to **41.3–59.7%**; at 154 patterns/s, improved processing recovered only approximately **12.5–37.6%**. Thus, throughput choices can change the usable fraction by tens of percentage points and make the final result strongly dependent on cleanup (pqac-00000009).

### Accelerating voltage

A controlled study varied **10, 20, and 30 kV**, with 20 kV as the training/default condition. At 10 kV many patterns were misclassified; 30 kV produced reasonably good classifications. Lower voltage widened Kikuchi bands and changed their apparent spacing, yielding one of the two parameter changes that caused broadly noteworthy performance losses (the other was one-frame acquisition) (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

For aluminum specifically, shot-peened 7075-T651 was examined at **5, 10, and 20 kV**, with **4×4 and 8×8 binning**. The study found dictionary indexing more robust than conventional Hough indexing for low-quality, low-voltage patterns, but did not report a complete numerical success-rate table for the acquisition sweep. This supports transferability to Al but also illustrates the scarcity of quantitative acquisition-response curves (pqac-00000008).

### Pattern exposure and binning/resolution

Pattern resolution was varied from **156×128** to **622×512** and **1244×1024 pixels**. Low-resolution acquisition retained high classification accuracy for most tested phases, but phases having similar structures were appreciably more sensitive. Thus, binning can accelerate mapping without a universal penalty, but its acceptability depends on the phase discrimination task (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

Commercial image-quality metrics should not be treated as instrument-independent confidence measures. Published analysis notes that vendors use different definitions of band contrast, pattern quality, and image quality; at least one definition was not disclosed, and the available definitions were only partly documented. Beam current, accelerating voltage, working distance, charging, holder stability, surface condition, orientation, and crystal perfection all affect these metrics, yet their relative contributions, reproducibility, and strain sensitivity had not been quantitatively characterized (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

### Phase-list selection

Phase-list choice can dominate otherwise ideal acquisition. For duplex steel, supplying the two correct phases produced a high-fidelity map. Supplying **12 candidate phases**—the two correct solutions plus ten crystallographically plausible alternatives—caused **not a single pattern** to index to either correct phase, even though the patterns were collected using the study’s ideal settings (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). This is highly relevant to LPBF Al-Si: adding α-Al, diamond-cubic Si, oxides, Mg₂Si, or metastable candidates without chemistry-informed constraints can create confident but false assignments.

### LPBF Al-Si evidence gap

The search recovered many EBSD applications to additively manufactured Al alloys, but not a controlled LPBF AlSi10Mg factorial study reporting indexing rate or confidence index against beam current, voltage, exposure, binning, and phase-list composition. Consequently, commonly published AlSi10Mg settings are examples rather than validated optima. This gap is a compelling funding need: LPBF Al-Si combines fine cellular α-Al/Si structure, high defect density, residual strain, pores, oxides, and polishing sensitivity, so generic EBSD defaults cannot be assumed to preserve phase and orientation fidelity.

## 3. Micro-XRF

### Tube voltage, current, and filters

A commercial portable-XRF alloy protocol used **15–50 kV** and **12–106 µA**, depending on the alloy class and concentration range. Automatic primary-beam filters included **75 µm Cu/25 µm Ti/200 µm Al**, **38 µm Al**, **25 µm Ti/300 µm Al**, and **25 µm Fe**. A **60 s** acquisition was divided into separate **30 s light-element and heavy-element scans** (pqac-00000028). These choices matter because tube voltage determines which absorption edges are excited, current controls incident flux, and filters trade continuum background against analyte-line intensity.

A micro-XRF component study operated at **40 kV/0.2 mA**, increased current from **0.2 to 1.0 mA** on an Ag-Cu alloy to test input-rate effects, and compared **12.5, 25, and 50 µm Mo** filters and **50 and 200 µm Al** filters. Polycapillary spectra were **35–40 times** more intense than monocapillary spectra; one optic provided an approximately **300-fold flux-density gain**, showing that sensitivity cannot be inferred from tube power alone (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

At **40 kV, 0.2 mA, and 1000 s**, reported micro-XRF minimum detection limits were typically **10–100 ppm**; examples were **23–68 ppm Mn**, **10–22 ppm Rb**, and **68–94 ppm Ca**, depending on tube and optics. These values are not universal alloy limits because atmosphere, optic transmission, detector window, filter, matrix, and live time all differ (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

### Matrix corrections and calibration

Fundamental-parameter correction does not eliminate matrix dependence. In a quantitative micro-XRF assessment, matrix-matched calibration reduced typical errors to **<5% for most major elements** and **<6% for some minor elements**. Without suitable standards, typical errors were below **50% for many major/minor elements** and reached **100% for trace elements**, with some relative errors exceeding 100% (pqac-00000007).

Metal-alloy measurements reinforce this point. Commercial EDXRF/WDXRF generally achieved absolute deviations below **1 wt% for matrix elements** and below **0.25 wt% for minor elements under 2 wt%**, but relative deviations above 100% occurred below 1 wt%. Mg in Al alloys produced the particularly large **40%** and **5000%** errors described above. The authors attributed the poor light-element performance to low Mg/Al/Si X-ray production cross-sections and strong absorption by air and the detector window (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029).

## 4. Why current practice remains expertise-dependent

The evidence supports a careful formulation: published practice is often **empirical, instrument-specific, and operator-mediated**, although the retrieved papers do not literally label every optimization procedure “trial-and-error.”

* The operator remains responsible for recognizing pile-up/escape artefacts, checking peak labels, and rejecting poor background fits; automated software does not remove this responsibility (pqac-00000017).
* EBSD operating values are explicitly described as non-fixed and valid over manufacturer-dependent ranges. Accurate Hough phase mapping presupposes that the operator already knows and supplies the correct phases; a broader but plausible list can yield zero correct phase assignments (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).
* Commercial EBSD quality metrics are vendor-specific, partly documented, and in at least one case not disclosed. The relative effects of current, voltage, surface condition, orientation, and other variables remain unquantified (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).
* Investigators comparing standardless EDS systems could not identify the cause of different accuracies because relevant hardware and analysis methods were manufacturer-constrained (pqac-00000019).

ASTM E1508 and ISO 22309 are therefore best characterized as supplying **minimum practices and operating constraints**, not transparent alloy-specific optimization models. The accessible evidence documents recommendations such as **overvoltage ≥1.8**, flat/polished geometry, and approximately **35° detector take-off**, but the retrieved literature does not provide the derivation, uncertainty surface, or validation data needed to translate those thresholds into optimal settings for a particular detector, alloy, microstructure, and analytical objective (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Claims that the standards contain “no rationale” would be too strong; the defensible proposal claim is that the rationale and quantitative response surfaces needed for specimen-specific optimization are **sparsely documented or not readily accessible**, particularly where vendor algorithms and calibration databases are proprietary.

## Proposal-ready needs statement

> SEM-based microanalysis lacks validated, transferable acquisition-response models linking controllable settings to ground-truth chemical and crystallographic fidelity in technologically important metal alloys. Standardless SEM-EDS may carry up to ±30% relative uncertainty, while standards-based analysis can approach ±5%; geometry, overvoltage, current, and dead time introduce additional coupled errors. EBSD acquisition speed alone has changed correct indexing from 34.9% to 9.3%, one-frame acquisition can misclassify nearly an entire map, and an over-inclusive phase list has produced zero correct phase assignments despite ideal patterns. In XRF alloy analysis, minor Mg has been overestimated by 40% and trace Mg by 5000%, while matrix-matched calibration can reduce major-element errors below 5%. Yet controlled, ground-truthed parameter sweeps are notably absent for LPBF AlSi10Mg. Standards and vendor guidance provide operating thresholds and defaults, but not transparent, alloy-specific uncertainty surfaces. Funding is therefore needed to develop factorial benchmark datasets and physics-informed decision tools that recommend voltage, dose/current, dead time, geometry, exposure/binning, filters, and phase lists while reporting expected uncertainty and indexing fidelity."}

For rigorous standards-based analysis, the NPL reference-alloy experiment limited measured beam-current drift to **0.2%** over a **20 min** acquisition session. Unnormalized standardless analysis likewise requires a stable current because a separately acquired reference spectrum normalizes current and detector geometry. Ratio-based methods that derive elemental ratios within the same spectrum can suppress current instability and have reported accuracy better than **5%**, but their calibration factors remain beam-energy dependent (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000020).

### Take-off geometry and specimen topography

The quantitative protocol requires a flat, polished surface normal to the beam and approximately **35° to the EDS detector**. In practical tests, holes and grooves substantially changed integrated counts and even the number of elements identified because low local take-off angles obstructed emitted X-rays (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000019). This is directly relevant to LPBF alloys: pores, melt-pool relief, incompletely polished Si particles, and tilted surfaces preferentially absorb low-energy Mg and Al X-rays.

### Minor/trace Mg in aluminum

The retrieved literature did **not** provide a controlled SEM-EDS parameter sweep for Mg in LPBF AlSi10Mg against certified bulk chemistry. That absence is itself an important proposal gap. The strongest defensible SEM-EDS statement is that standardless errors can reach **±30%**, light-element uncertainty is greater, and normalized output can conceal missing mass (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020).

Closely analogous XRF alloy evidence shows how severe the Al-matrix/light-element problem can become: Mg in AlMg4.5Mn0.7 was over-reported by approximately **2 wt%**, or **40% relative**, while nominal Al99.5 was reported as **0.196 wt% Mg instead of 0.004 wt%**, a **5000% relative deviation**. These are XRF rather than SEM-EDS results and must not be presented as SEM-EDS performance, but they quantitatively demonstrate why trace Mg in an Al matrix requires matrix-matched validation rather than reliance on an automatic alloy mode (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029).

## 2. EBSD indexing and confidence

### Beam current and exposure

Beam current and exposure jointly determine electron dose and pattern signal-to-noise ratio. Direct current sweeps were not recovered for LPBF AlSi10Mg, but controlled frame-averaging data quantify the dose/throughput tradeoff. A study varied averaging among **1, 5, 10, 20, and 30 frames** over **3,848 patterns** in a duplex alloy. At one frame, essentially all patterns were misclassified; five improved the result, ten produced a reasonable fraction of correct classifications, and 20–30 produced nearly complete agreement with the reference phase map. Reducing averaging from 30 to five made acquisition **six times faster** while retaining high accuracy for most tested phases, but the most crystallographically similar phases remained vulnerable (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

Independent conventional-indexing data show the consequence of faster acquisition. Increasing collection rate from **54 to 154 patterns/s** reduced correctly indexed patterns from **34.9% to 9.3%**. At 54 patterns/s, rescanning or neighbor-based processing increased success to **41.3–59.7%**; at 154 patterns/s, improved processing recovered only approximately **12.5–37.6%**. Thus, throughput choices can change the usable fraction by tens of percentage points and make the final result strongly dependent on cleanup (pqac-00000009).

### Accelerating voltage

A controlled study varied **10, 20, and 30 kV**, with 20 kV as the training/default condition. At 10 kV many patterns were misclassified; 30 kV produced reasonably good classifications. Lower voltage widened Kikuchi bands and changed their apparent spacing, yielding one of the two parameter changes that caused broadly noteworthy performance losses (the other was one-frame acquisition) (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

For aluminum specifically, shot-peened 7075-T651 was examined at **5, 10, and 20 kV**, with **4×4 and 8×8 binning**. The study found dictionary indexing more robust than conventional Hough indexing for low-quality, low-voltage patterns, but did not report a complete numerical success-rate table for the acquisition sweep. This supports transferability to Al but also illustrates the scarcity of quantitative acquisition-response curves (pqac-00000008).

### Pattern exposure and binning/resolution

Pattern resolution was varied from **156×128** to **622×512** and **1244×1024 pixels**. Low-resolution acquisition retained high classification accuracy for most tested phases, but phases having similar structures were appreciably more sensitive. Thus, binning can accelerate mapping without a universal penalty, but its acceptability depends on the phase discrimination task (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

Commercial image-quality metrics should not be treated as instrument-independent confidence measures. Published analysis notes that vendors use different definitions of band contrast, pattern quality, and image quality; at least one definition was not disclosed, and the available definitions were only partly documented. Beam current, accelerating voltage, working distance, charging, holder stability, surface condition, orientation, and crystal perfection all affect these metrics, yet their relative contributions, reproducibility, and strain sensitivity had not been quantitatively characterized (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

### Phase-list selection

Phase-list choice can dominate otherwise ideal acquisition. For duplex steel, supplying the two correct phases produced a high-fidelity map. Supplying **12 candidate phases**—the two correct solutions plus ten crystallographically plausible alternatives—caused **not a single pattern** to index to either correct phase, even though the patterns were collected using the study’s ideal settings (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). This is highly relevant to LPBF Al-Si: adding α-Al, diamond-cubic Si, oxides, Mg₂Si, or metastable candidates without chemistry-informed constraints can create confident but false assignments.

### LPBF Al-Si evidence gap

The search recovered many EBSD applications to additively manufactured Al alloys, but not a controlled LPBF AlSi10Mg factorial study reporting indexing rate or confidence index against beam current, voltage, exposure, binning, and phase-list composition. Consequently, commonly published AlSi10Mg settings are examples rather than validated optima. This gap is a compelling funding need: LPBF Al-Si combines fine cellular α-Al/Si structure, high defect density, residual strain, pores, oxides, and polishing sensitivity, so generic EBSD defaults cannot be assumed to preserve phase and orientation fidelity.

## 3. Micro-XRF

### Tube voltage, current, and filters

A commercial portable-XRF alloy protocol used **15–50 kV** and **12–106 µA**, depending on the alloy class and concentration range. Automatic primary-beam filters included **75 µm Cu/25 µm Ti/200 µm Al**, **38 µm Al**, **25 µm Ti/300 µm Al**, and **25 µm Fe**. A **60 s** acquisition was divided into separate **30 s light-element and heavy-element scans** (pqac-00000028). These choices matter because tube voltage determines which absorption edges are excited, current controls incident flux, and filters trade continuum background against analyte-line intensity.

A micro-XRF component study operated at **40 kV/0.2 mA**, increased current from **0.2 to 1.0 mA** on an Ag-Cu alloy to test input-rate effects, and compared **12.5, 25, and 50 µm Mo** filters and **50 and 200 µm Al** filters. Polycapillary spectra were **35–40 times** more intense than monocapillary spectra; one optic provided an approximately **300-fold flux-density gain**, showing that sensitivity cannot be inferred from tube power alone (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

At **40 kV, 0.2 mA, and 1000 s**, reported micro-XRF minimum detection limits were typically **10–100 ppm**; examples were **23–68 ppm Mn**, **10–22 ppm Rb**, and **68–94 ppm Ca**, depending on tube and optics. These values are not universal alloy limits because atmosphere, optic transmission, detector window, filter, matrix, and live time all differ (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

### Matrix corrections and calibration

Fundamental-parameter correction does not eliminate matrix dependence. In a quantitative micro-XRF assessment, matrix-matched calibration reduced typical errors to **<5% for most major elements** and **<6% for some minor elements**. Without suitable standards, typical errors were below **50% for many major/minor elements** and reached **100% for trace elements**, with some relative errors exceeding 100% (pqac-00000007).

Metal-alloy measurements reinforce this point. Commercial EDXRF/WDXRF generally achieved absolute deviations below **1 wt% for matrix elements** and below **0.25 wt% for minor elements under 2 wt%**, but relative deviations above 100% occurred below 1 wt%. Mg in Al alloys produced the particularly large **40%** and **5000%** errors described above. The authors attributed the poor light-element performance to low Mg/Al/Si X-ray production cross-sections and strong absorption by air and the detector window (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029).

## 4. Why current practice remains expertise-dependent

The evidence supports a careful formulation: published practice is often **empirical, instrument-specific, and operator-mediated**, although the retrieved papers do not literally label every optimization procedure “trial-and-error.”

* The operator remains responsible for recognizing pile-up/escape artefacts, checking peak labels, and rejecting poor background fits; automated software does not remove this responsibility (pqac-00000017).
* EBSD operating values are explicitly described as non-fixed and valid over manufacturer-dependent ranges. Accurate Hough phase mapping presupposes that the operator already knows and supplies the correct phases; a broader but plausible list can yield zero correct phase assignments (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).
* Commercial EBSD quality metrics are vendor-specific, partly documented, and in at least one case not disclosed. The relative effects of current, voltage, surface condition, orientation, and other variables remain unquantified (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).
* Investigators comparing standardless EDS systems could not identify the cause of different accuracies because relevant hardware and analysis methods were manufacturer-constrained (pqac-00000019).

ASTM E1508 and ISO 22309 are therefore best characterized as supplying **minimum practices and operating constraints**, not transparent alloy-specific optimization models. The accessible evidence documents recommendations such as **overvoltage ≥1.8**, flat/polished geometry, and approximately **35° detector take-off**, but the retrieved literature does not provide the derivation, uncertainty surface, or validation data needed to translate those thresholds into optimal settings for a particular detector, alloy, microstructure, and analytical objective (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Claims that the standards contain “no rationale” would be too strong; the defensible proposal claim is that the rationale and quantitative response surfaces needed for specimen-specific optimization are **sparsely documented or not readily accessible**, particularly where vendor algorithms and calibration databases are proprietary.

## Proposal-ready needs statement

Standardless SEM-EDS may carry up to ±30% relative uncertainty, while standards-based analysis can approach ±5%; geometry, overvoltage, current, and dead time introduce additional coupled errors. EBSD acquisition speed alone has changed correct indexing from 34.9% to 9.3%, one-frame acquisition can misclassify nearly an entire map, and an over-inclusive phase list has produced zero correct phase assignments despite ideal patterns. In XRF alloy analysis, minor Mg has been overestimated by 40% and trace Mg by 5000%, while matrix-matched calibration can reduce major-element errors below 5%. Yet controlled, ground-truthed parameter sweeps are notably absent for LPBF AlSi10Mg. Standards and vendor guidance provide operating thresholds and defaults, but not transparent, alloy-specific uncertainty surfaces. Funding is therefore needed to develop factorial benchmark datasets and physics-informed decision tools that recommend voltage, dose/current, dead time, geometry, exposure/binning, filters, and phase lists while reporting expected uncertainty and indexing fidelity."}

# Quantitative evidence for a funding-proposal needs statement

## Executive conclusion

Acquisition settings are not merely operational details: they determine whether SEM-EDS returns approximately quantitative chemistry or a normalized but biased composition, whether EBSD maps contain mostly correct orientations or mostly failed/misassigned pixels, and whether micro-XRF detects minor alloying additions or overestimates them by orders of magnitude. The literature supports a strong need for **alloy-, instrument-, and task-specific acquisition-response models**, especially for LPBF Al-Si-Mg, because controlled factorial studies connecting settings to ground-truth fidelity are sparse.

| **SEM-EDS: accelerating voltage/overvoltage** | ISO 22309 specifies incident energy of at least **1.8× the selected X-ray-line energy**; adequate Fe-K excitation, for example, requires at least **12 kV**. Measurements at **5, 10, and 20 kV** produced substantial composition scatter in a low-energy-line test material. | Voltage determines excitation efficiency and interaction volume; one fixed voltage is not valid for every alloying element. | (tong2026measurementuncertaintiesof pages 8-11, tong2026measurementuncertaintiesof pages 18-21) |
| **SEM-EDS: take-off geometry** | Quantitative protocols require a flat surface normal to the beam and approximately **35° to the EDS detector**. Low take-off angles at holes and grooves reduced integral counts and the number of detected elements. | Tilt, roughness, pores, and melt-pool relief can create element-dependent absorption errors, especially for low-energy Mg and Al lines. | (kallio2025accuracyandprecision pages 59-62, tong2026measurementuncertaintiesof pages 18-21) |
| **SEM-EDS: beam current/dead time** | Beam current and dead time were identified as dominant variables; **10–20% dead time** was recommended. In standards-based work, beam-current drift was held to **0.2%** over a **20 min** session. | Too little current gives poor counting statistics, while excessive rate causes pile-up and dead-time losses; current must be measured or controlled. | (kallio2025accuracyandprecision pages 59-62, tong2026measurementuncertaintiesof pages 21-24) |

### Standards-based versus standardless accuracy

Commercial image-quality metrics should not be treated as instrument-independent confidence measures. Published analysis notes that vendors use different definitions of band contrast, pattern quality, and image quality; at least one definition was not disclosed, and the available definitions were only partly documented. Beam current, accelerating voltage, working distance, charging, holder stability, surface condition, orientation, and crystal perfection all affect these metrics, yet their relative contributions, reproducibility, and strain sensitivity had not been quantitatively characterized (cocle2008developmentofthe pages 26-31, cocle2008developmentofthe pages 31-34).

Phase-list choice can dominate otherwise ideal acquisition. For duplex steel, supplying the two correct phases produced a high-fidelity map. The search recovered many EBSD applications to additively manufactured Al alloys, but not a controlled LPBF AlSi10Mg factorial study reporting indexing rate or confidence index against beam current, voltage, exposure, binning, and phase-list composition. Consequently, commonly published AlSi10Mg settings are examples rather than validated optima. ## 3. Micro-XRF

### Tube voltage, current, and filters

A commercial portable-XRF alloy protocol used **15–50 kV** and **12–106 µA**, depending on the alloy class and concentration range. Automatic primary-beam filters included **75 µm Cu/25 µm Ti/200 µm Al**, **38 µm Al**, **25 µm Ti/300 µm Al**, and **25 µm Fe**. A **60 s** acquisition was divided into separate **30 s light-element and heavy-element scans** (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 4-5). These choices matter because tube voltage determines which absorption edges are excited, current controls incident flux, and filters trade continuum background against analyte-line intensity.

A micro-XRF component study operated at **40 kV/0.2 mA**, increased current from **0.2 to 1.0 mA** on an Ag-Cu alloy to test input-rate effects, and compared **12.5, 25, and 50 µm Mo** filters and **50 and 200 µm Al** filters.
